OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Urogenital Pro:
What & Why

Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) = descent of one or more pelvic organs into the vagina due to weakness of the pelvic floor support — the fascia, ligaments and muscles give way, and the vaginal walls (with the organ behind them) bulge downwards. It’s very common — up to 40% of postmenopausal women — and, while not dangerous, it causes significant quality-of-life impairment (pressure, urinary, bowel, sexual symptoms).

The core mechanism: the pelvic organs are held up by the pelvic floor (levator ani) muscles + endopelvic fascia/ligaments. Childbirth, ageing and oestrogen loss weaken these → the organs descend, pushing the vaginal walls ahead of them. This is why the risk factors are all things that weaken/damage the pelvic floor, and why strengthening it (PFMT) and supporting it (pessary) are first-line.
Examinable essence: classify by compartment (which organ/wall), and manage in a stepwise conservative → pessary → surgical ladder, with surgery matched to the compartment.

A urethrocele = urethral descent; often combined as a cysto-urethrocele.
Risk Factors (anything that weakens the pelvic floor)
  • Increasing age and menopause (oestrogen loss weakens tissues)
  • Multiparity and vaginal deliveries (the biggest — especially instrumental/prolonged, large babies)
  • Obesity (chronic raised intra-abdominal pressure)
  • Chronic cough / chronic constipation / heavy lifting (raised intra-abdominal pressure)
  • Spina bifida / connective tissue disorders (Ehlers-Danlos)
  • Previous pelvic surgery (e.g. hysterectomy → vault prolapse)
Clinical Features
  • A sensation of pressure, heaviness, or “something coming down” / “bearing down” — the hallmark; worse at the end of the day or on standing
  • A palpable/visible vaginal lump or bulge
  • Urinary symptoms: incontinence, frequency, urgency, incomplete emptying (cystocele)
  • Bowel symptoms: constipation, incomplete evacuation, splinting (rectocele)
  • Sexual dysfunction — discomfort, reduced sensation
Assessment (NICE NG123)
  • Speculum/bimanual examination (a Sims speculum helps visualise each wall) — assess which compartment, examining while the woman bears down and, if needed, standing (prolapse may only show upright)
  • Assess pelvic floor strength, look for vaginal atrophy, and rule out a pelvic mass
  • Staging — POP-Q (Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification), or the older Baden-Walker grading; broadly graded by how far the leading edge descends relative to the hymen
  • Investigate further (urodynamics, bowel studies) if significant urinary/bowel symptoms
Management (NICE NG123)
1️⃣ Conservative (first-line)
  • Asymptomatic → no treatment needed (observation is reasonable)
  • Lifestyle: weight loss, treat constipation + chronic cough, avoid heavy lifting
  • Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) — supervised, ≥16 weeks; most useful for mild (POP-Q stage 1–2)
  • Topical (vaginal) oestrogen — for associated vaginal atrophy
2️⃣ Pessary
  • Vaginal pessary (e.g. ring) — supports the prolapse, sitting around the cervix/vault
  • Offer to any woman with symptomatic prolapse — especially if she wishes to preserve fertility, is unfit for surgery, or prefers to avoid it
  • Remove/change at least every 6 months (prevent erosion, discharge, bleeding, fistula)
3️⃣ Surgery (definitive — symptoms persist or conservative declined) — matched to compartment
CompartmentProcedure
Cystocele / anterior wallAnterior colporrhaphy (anterior repair, without mesh)
Rectocele / posterior wallPosterior colporrhaphy (posterior repair, without mesh)
Uterine prolapseVaginal hysterectomy (± apical support) or sacrohysteropexy (uterus-preserving)
Vault prolapseSacrocolpopexy (abdominal/laparoscopic, with mesh) or sacrospinous fixation
Frail, not retaining sexual functionColpocleisis (vaginal closure)
Vaginal mesh caution: transvaginal mesh for prolapse is associated with serious complications (mesh erosion, chronic pain) and its use is now highly restricted/paused in the UK (research-only per NICE IPG599). Native-tissue (non-mesh) repairs are first-line, with mesh reserved for specific procedures (e.g. sacrocolpopexy) after MDT discussion + a decision aid. 6-month post-op review (check for mesh exposure if mesh used).

Descent of pelvic organs into the vagina from pelvic floor weakness; ~40% of postmenopausal women.
Compartments
Cystocele (bladder, anterior), rectocele (rectum, posterior → constipation), uterine, vault (post-hysterectomy), enterocele.
Risk factors
Vaginal delivery/multiparity (biggest), age/menopause, obesity, raised intra-abdominal pressure.
Classic symptom
“Something coming down” / bearing-down sensation ± urinary/bowel symptoms.
Examine
With the woman bearing down (± standing); stage with POP-Q.
Management ladder
Conservative (weight loss, PFMT, topical oestrogen) → pessary (ring; change every 6 months) → surgery.

Mesh

Asymptomatic
No treatment.
OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Termination of:
What & Why

Termination of pregnancy (TOP) = the medical or surgical ending of a pregnancy. It’s common, essential healthcare with a specific UK legal framework you must know, and the methods (medical vs surgical), gestational limits, and aftercare (anti-D, contraception) are examinable.

The whole topic hangs on two things: the legal grounds and choosing the method by gestation.
The Legal Framework (Abortion Act 1967, as amended)
  • Abortion in England, Scotland and Wales is governed by the Abortion Act 1967 (as amended by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990)
  • Upper limit for most abortions is 24 weeks (23⁺⁶)
  • Two registered medical practitioners must agree, in good faith, that a legal ground is met (one is sufficient in an emergency — to save the woman’s life or prevent grave permanent injury)
The grounds (A–E)
GroundBasisTime limit
AContinuing risks the woman’s lifeNo limit
BPrevent grave permanent injury to her physical/mental healthNo limit
CGreater risk to the woman’s physical/mental health than termination — the ground used for the vast majority<24 weeks
DGreater risk to the physical/mental health of existing children<24 weeks
ESubstantial risk of serious fetal abnormalityNo limit
No upper limit applies for Grounds A, B and E (risk to life, grave injury, serious fetal abnormality).
🗺️ Northern Ireland
  • Separate framework (Abortion (NI) Regulations 2020) — broadly up to ~12 weeks on request, with different certification
📱 Telemedicine / “pills by post”
  • Since the COVID provisions were made permanent (2022), early medical abortion at home (up to 9⁺⁶ weeks) can follow a remote consultation, with both mifepristone + misoprostol taken at home
Assessment Before TOP (NICE NG140)
  • Confirm and date the pregnancy — ultrasound as needed (gestation determines method + legal ground)
  • Bloods — blood group & Rhesus status, FBC
  • STI screening (chlamydia and others)
  • Discuss options non-judgementally, obtain informed consent, offer counselling/support
  • Discuss future contraception — to be started immediately after
The Decisive Fork — Medical vs Surgical

Both are options up to 23⁺⁶ weeks; choice depends on gestation and patient preference.

💊 Medical TOP
  • Mifepristone (anti-progesterone) — blocks progesterone → breaks down the decidua, sensitises the uterus
  • Misoprostol (prostaglandin analogue) — given 24–48 h later → uterine contractions expel the pregnancy
  • Suitable across gestations (early medical abortion; higher gestations use repeated misoprostol)
🔧 Surgical TOP
  • Vacuum aspiration — manual (MVA) or electric (EVA) — typically up to ~14 weeks
  • Dilatation & evacuation (D&E) — later gestations (after ~14 weeks)
  • Cervical priming with misoprostol ± mifepristone beforehand (softens/dilates cervix, reduces trauma)
  • Under local, conscious sedation, or general anaesthesia
Confirming success (medical): follow-up pregnancy test at ~2 weeks, ideally a multi-level/quantitative (serum β-hCG) test. A urine test can stay positive up to ~4 weeks; a positive test beyond 4 weeks suggests incomplete abortion or persistent trophoblast (→ investigate: ?retained products, ?GTD).
Aftercare
💉 Anti-D prophylaxis
  • Give to RhD-negative women having a surgical abortion, and medical abortion after 10 weeks
  • No longer required for early medical abortion before 10 weeks (currency update — the old “after 10 weeks” rule reflects the medical route; the surgical rule differs)
🔄 Immediate contraception
  • IUD/IUS can be inserted immediately after surgical evacuation
  • Implant, injection or pills can be started at the time of medical TOP
  • Analgesia and safety-netting for complications
  • No routine follow-up needed if the pregnancy test/protocol confirms success (NICE NG140)
Complications
  • Incomplete abortion / retained products (may need a repeat procedure)
  • Infection (endometritis)
  • Haemorrhage
  • Uterine perforation (surgical), cervical trauma
  • Failed termination / continuing pregnancy
  • Psychological impact (support should be available)
Exam Pearls
Legal framework
Abortion Act 1967 (as amended); most abortions ≤24 weeks; TWO doctors agree (one in emergency).
Grounds
A–E: “C” (risk to woman’s health <24 wks) is commonest; “E” (serious fetal abnormality) has NO time limit.
Telemedicine
Pills-by-post now permanent for early medical abortion ≤9⁺⁶ weeks (both pills at home).
Medical TOP
Mifepristone (anti-progesterone) → misoprostol (prostaglandin) 24–48 h later.
Surgical TOP
Vacuum aspiration (MVA/EVA) up to ~14 wks; D&E later; cervical priming with misoprostol ± mifepristone first.
Confirm success
β-hCG/multi-level test at 2 weeks. Urine test positive up to 4 weeks; positive beyond 4 weeks → incomplete/retained/persistent trophoblast.
Anti-D
RhD-negative → surgical abortion, or medical >10 weeks. NOT needed for early medical <10 weeks now.
Contraception
Start immediately (IUD/IUS post-evacuation).
Complications
Retained products, infection, haemorrhage, perforation, failed TOP.
OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Reduced Fetal:
What & Why

Reduced fetal movements (RFM) = a decrease or cessation of the mother’s perception of her baby’s movements. It matters because it can be a warning sign of fetal compromise — a hypoxic fetus reduces its activity to conserve oxygen — and RFM is associated with stillbirth and fetal growth restriction (FGR). It’s one of the commonest reasons women contact maternity services; the skill is a structured, gestation-dependent workup to catch the few compromised babies without over-investigating the well majority.

The core physiological logic: a fetus with chronic hypoxia redistributes blood to vital organs and reduces movement to lower oxygen consumption — a compensatory mechanism. So RFM is a non-specific but important surrogate marker of fetal condition; the job is to work out whether this baby is compensating or just having a quiet spell.
Physiology of Fetal Movements
  • Quickening (first perception) at ~18–20 weeks (earlier in multiparous women)
  • Movements increase until ~32 weeks, then plateau — they change in character but should NOT reduce at the end of pregnancy (the myth that late movements decrease is wrong)
  • There is no single normal number — each baby has its own pattern
Causes — Benign Perception vs Genuine Compromise
📷 Image placeholder — Benign/perceptual causes (anterior placenta, anterior fetal position, obesity, sedatives, distraction) vs concerning/pathological (SGA/FGR, placental insufficiency, oligohydramnios, hypoxia, fetomaternal haemorrhage)
🟢 Benign / perceptual
  • Posture / distraction / being busy (movements more noticeable lying down + focused)
  • Anterior placenta (<28 weeks — cushions movements)
  • Anterior fetal position (movements directed backwards)
  • Maternal body habitus (obesity → harder to feel)
  • Medication — alcohol + sedatives temporarily reduce movements
🔴 Concerning / pathological
  • Fetal growth restriction / SGA — linked with ~29% of RFM cases
  • Placental insufficiency, oligohydramnios (polyhydramnios can also alter perception)
  • Fetal hypoxia / distress, impending stillbirth
  • Fetomaternal haemorrhage, infection

Advice to Give the Mother (RCOG)
If concerned about reduced movements after 28 weeks: lie on the left side and focus on movements for 2 hours — if <10 movements in 2 hours, contact the maternity unit immediately.
Do NOT wait until the next day and do NOT rely on home Doppler/apps for reassurance.
Management (RCOG)
  • Investigations normal (normal CTG + normal growth/liquor): reassure; advise to re-present immediately if RFM recurs (recurrent RFM warrants ultrasound + closer surveillance)
  • CTG abnormal: senior obstetric review; decisions about delivery weigh gestation against the degree of abnormality
  • SGA / abnormal Doppler / abnormal liquor: manage as FGR (RCOG Green-top 31) — increased surveillance, timed delivery
  • Recurrent RFM is itself a risk factor → lower threshold for scanning + delivery discussion near term
Evidence caveat — the AFFIRM trial: a formal “awareness of fetal movements” care package did NOT significantly reduce stillbirth — and increased inductions and caesareans. So routine formal kick-counting with fixed alarm limits is NOT recommended; instead, women are advised to be aware of their baby’s individual pattern and report any reduction.
Exam Pearls
Significance
RFM can signal fetal compromise — the fetus reduces movement to conserve O₂ in chronic hypoxia. Associated with stillbirth and FGR.
Physiology
Quickening ~18–20 weeks; movements plateau (not reduce) after 32 weeks. Late-pregnancy movements should NOT decrease.
Benign vs concerning
Benign ↓perception: anterior placenta, anterior fetal position, obesity, sedatives/alcohol, distraction. Concerning: SGA/FGR (~29%), placental insufficiency, oligohydramnios.
Workup by gestation
<24 wks never felt → fetal medicine; 24–28 → Doppler + risk history; >28 → Doppler (no heartbeat = immediate USS) → CTG ≥20 min → USS (growth/liquor/Doppler) if concern.
Advice
After 28 wks: lie left, focus 2 hours; <10 movements → contact unit NOW. Don’t wait; don’t use home Doppler.
AFFIRM
Formal kick-counting packages don’t reduce stillbirth (and raise intervention) → be aware of individual pattern, report reductions.
Recurrence
Recurrent RFM → ultrasound + closer surveillance.
OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ovarian Torsio:
What & Why

Ovarian torsion = a gynaecological surgical emergency in which the ovary (usually with the fallopian tube — “adnexal torsion”) twists around its supporting ligaments, cutting off its blood supply. It threatens the viability of the ovary — delayed diagnosis → infarction and loss of ovarian tissue with fertility consequences — and it’s a classic acute pelvic pain differential that’s easy to miss (overlaps with appendicitis, ectopic, and ovarian cyst accident).

The exam essence: suspect it clinically, image with ultrasound, and operate promptly — don’t be reassured by normal Doppler flow.
The core mechanism: the ovary hangs on two ligaments — the infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament (carrying the ovarian vessels) and the utero-ovarian ligament. Twisting first occludes the low-pressure venous + lymphatic drainage → ovarian congestion + oedema (enlargement) → then, as swelling worsens, arterial inflow is compromised → ischaemia → infarction.
This venous-first sequence is why arterial Doppler flow can still be present in early/partial torsion — the key diagnostic trap.
The Decisive Fork — Is There an Ovarian Mass?

Torsion almost always happens to an enlarged/abnormal ovary — a mass acts as a lever point.

Torsion with a mass/cyst (~85–95%)Torsion of a normal ovary
WhoAdult with an ovarian cyst / dermoid / tumourPrepubertal girls (longer ligaments, mobile ovaries)
NoteA ~5 cm cyst is a classic size for torsionLess common but recognised
Key risk-factor logic: anything that enlarges or makes the ovary more mobile predisposes to torsion.
Risk Factors
  • Ovarian cyst or mass (the biggest — especially dermoid cysts, and cysts ~5 cm+)
  • Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) / ovulation induction (enlarged ovaries)
  • Pregnancy (corpus luteum cyst, ligament laxity)
  • Reproductive age (most cases)
  • Prepubertal girls (long ovarian ligaments, mobile ovaries)
  • Previous torsion
Presentation
  • Sudden-onset, severe, unilateral lower abdominal/pelvic pain — the cardinal feature
  • Often colicky or intermittent (if the ovary partially twists and untwists) then constant
  • Nausea and vomiting (prominent — vagal/peritoneal)
  • Pain may radiate to the flank/groin
  • Adnexal tenderness ± a palpable mass on examination
  • Low-grade fever, mild leukocytosis possible
Classic stem: young woman, sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain + vomiting, known ovarian cyst → ovarian torsion until proven otherwise.
Investigations
🚨 Always first
  • Pregnancy test (β-hCG) — always — exclude ectopic pregnancy (the must-not-miss differential)
🩸 Bloods
  • FBC (leukocytosis), CRP
Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler — first-line imaging
  • Enlarged, oedematous ovary (the commonest finding) ± an underlying cyst/mass
  • Peripherally displaced follicles (“string of pearls” around a swollen stroma)
  • “Whirlpool sign” — the twisted vascular pedicle
  • Free pelvic fluid
Doppler flow may be NORMAL or present in up to ~50% of torsions (venous obstruction precedes arterial) — normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion. A high-yield trap.
Definitive diagnosis is at surgery — if clinical suspicion is high despite equivocal imaging, proceed to diagnostic laparoscopy.
Management
Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency — the treatment is prompt surgery, usually laparoscopy.
🔧 Detorsion + conserve (preferred)
  • Laparoscopy (or laparotomy) to visualise and untwist (detort) the ovary
  • Ovarian conservation is now preferred in premenopausal women — even if the ovary looks ischaemic / “blue-black”
  • Intra-operative visual assessment of viability is highly inaccurate (only ~18–20% of “necrotic-looking” ovaries are truly necrotic; blackened ovaries frequently recover follicular function) → conserving preserves fertility
➕ Adjuncts
  • Cystectomy — remove an underlying cyst at the same time (once detorted)
  • Oophoropexy (fixing the ovary) — for recurrent torsion or torsion of a normal ovary with long ligaments
🔪 Oophorectomy — reserved cases
  • A frankly necrotic / non-viable ovary, or a suspicious mass (?malignancy)
  • Particularly in postmenopausal women
Timing is everything — the sooner detorsion happens, the greater the chance of salvaging the ovary.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Surgical emergency — twists on the infundibulopelvic + utero-ovarian ligaments → venous congestion first, then arterial ischaemia.
Classic stem
Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain + vomiting in a woman with an ovarian cyst (~5 cm).
Always
β-hCG — exclude ectopic.
Imaging
USS with Doppler is first-line: enlarged oedematous ovary, whirlpool sign, peripheral follicles.
The #1 trap
NORMAL Doppler flow does NOT exclude torsion (venous obstruction precedes arterial).
Treatment
Prompt laparoscopy + DETORSION, conserving the ovary — even if it looks ischaemic (visual viability assessment is unreliable).
Oophorectomy
Only for a truly necrotic ovary or suspected malignancy.
Who torses what
Prepubertal girls torse NORMAL ovaries (long ligaments); adults usually torse a MASS.
Risk factors
OHSS, pregnancy, ovulation induction, dermoid cysts.
OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Normal Labour:
What & Why

Antenatal care = the structured programme of monitoring throughout pregnancy that keeps mother and baby well, screens for complications, and prepares for birth. It matters because the schedule and its checks are a fixed, examinable framework — the booking bloods, the scans, the supplement advice, and the “what’s checked when” timetable are all high-yield recall.

Number of appointments: 10 for nulliparous, 7 for parous women (uncomplicated pregnancy). Guideline-verified — NICE NG201.

Booking Bloods

Supplements
💊 Folic acid
  • 400 mcg daily — from before conception to 12 weeks (reduces neural tube defects)
  • 5 mg (high dose) if: obesity, epilepsy (on antiepileptics), personal/family history of NTD, coeliac disease, diabetes, thalassaemia trait
☀️ Vitamin D
  • 10 micrograms daily — for ALL pregnant women (note the unit is micrograms, not mg)
🩸 Iron
  • Not routinely offered — only if anaemic
Vitamin A — teratogenic
  • Avoid vitamin A supplements and liver (teratogenic at high doses — well above the ~700 mcg daily requirement)
Lifestyle & Monitoring
  • BP at every appointment — refer >20 weeks with new BP ≥140/90 within 24h; ≥160/110 same-day
  • BP physiologically FALLS in the first half of pregnancy (vasodilation + increased volume), returning to baseline by term
  • Fetal movements — discuss after 24 weeks; advise to report reduced movements
  • SFH from 24–28 weeks — plot for growth; if small → growth scan
  • Alcohol (avoid completely), smoking cessation, healthy diet

Appointments
10 nulliparous / 7 parous (uncomplicated).
Booking bloods
FBC, group & Rhesus, antibodies, haemoglobinopathies, hep B, syphilis, HIV, urine culture (NOT rubella since 2016).
Supplements
Folic acid 400 mcg (5 mg if high-risk — obese / epilepsy / NTD / diabetes / coeliac / thalassaemia) + vitamin D 10 mcg for all.
Anti-D + ECV
Anti-D at 28 & 34 weeks if RhD-negative; check presentation + offer ECV at 36 weeks.
Scans
Dating (10–13⁺⁶), combined test (11–13⁺⁶), anomaly (18–20⁺⁶).
What & Why

Labour = the process of expelling the fetus, placenta and membranes — regular painful uterine contractions producing progressive cervical change. It matters because the three stages (and the mechanism of the second stage) are core exam material, and because recognising normal progress is what lets you detect the abnormal (failure to progress, fetal distress).

Diagnosis of Labour
Regular, painful uterine contractions + progressive cervical change (effacement and dilatation).

Distinguish from false labour / Braxton Hicks — irregular contractions, ~every 20 min, NO progressive cervical change → reassure and (if term, well) send home.

Other signs: a “show” (blood-stained mucus plug), rupture of the membranes.

The Three Stages of Labour (NICE NG235)

1️⃣ First stage — onset → full dilatation (10 cm)

  • Active / established phase — from ~4 cm; regular contractions, cervix dilates ~0.5–1 cm/hour, to full dilatation
2️⃣ Second stage — full dilatation → delivery of baby
  • Passive phase — full dilatation before/without an urge to push
  • Active phase — active pushing → delivery
  • Where the mechanism of labour (cardinal movements) occurs
3️⃣ Third stage — delivery of baby → delivery of placenta & membranes
  • Active management (recommended): prophylactic uterotonic (IM oxytocin / Syntocinon) + controlled cord traction + delayed cord clamping → reduces PPH risk
  • Physiological management: no drugs, spontaneous delivery of the placenta — only if uncomplicated and the woman chooses
Guideline-verified — NICE NG235: active third-stage management (IM oxytocin + controlled cord traction) reduces postpartum haemorrhage.

Labour = regular painful contractions + progressive cervical change (vs Braxton Hicks = no cervical change).
Stages
1st: onset → 10 cm (latent <4 cm; active ~0.5–1 cm/hr). 2nd: full dilatation → baby. 3rd: baby → placenta.

Active management (IM oxytocin + controlled cord traction) reduces PPH.

Engagement → descent → flexion → internal rotation → extension → restitution → external rotation → expulsion.

Partogram tracks progress; intermittent auscultation (low-risk) vs continuous CTG (high-risk).
Failure to progress
3 P’s — Power (commonest), Passage, Passenger.
OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Multiple Pregn:
What & Why

A multiple pregnancy = one carrying more than one fetus — most commonly twins. It is a high-risk pregnancy across the board: higher rates of nearly every obstetric complication (preterm birth, growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, PPH) plus, for one specific type, a set of dangerous shared-placenta complications requiring intensive fetal-medicine surveillance. Rates have risen with assisted conception (IVF) and older maternal age.

The single organising concept: chorionicity (how many placentas) — NOT zygosity — determines the risk profile and management, because it decides whether the babies share a circulation.
The Decisive Fork — Chorionicity (NOT Zygosity)

Classifying twins by zygosity (identical vs non-identical) is the biology; the clinically decisive classification is chorionicity + amnionicity (how many placentas and sacs), because that determines whether the babies share a circulation.

Zygosity — the biology
👥 Dizygotic (non-identical)
  • 2 ova fertilised by 2 sperm → always DCDA (2 placentas, 2 sacs)
  • ~2/3 of twins
🧬 Monozygotic (identical)
  • 1 fertilised ovum splits
  • The TIMING of the split determines chorionicity → can be DCDA, MCDA or MCMA
Chorionicity — what matters clinically

OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Female Genital:
Definition & The Core Concept

Female genital mutilation (FGM) = all procedures involving PARTIAL or TOTAL REMOVAL of the external female genitalia, or other injury to the female genital organs, for NON-MEDICAL reasons. It has NO health benefits, causes serious physical + psychological harm, is a form of CHILD ABUSE + a human-rights violation, and is ILLEGAL in the UK.

The core concept — a safeguarding + legal + clinical issue rolled into one. Three threads: (1) CLASSIFY it (the WHO Types 1–4 — what was done); (2) know the LEGAL framework — FGM is illegal (FGM Act 2003), there is an FGM PROTECTION ORDER for girls at risk, and a MANDATORY REPORTING DUTY to report KNOWN cases in under-18s to the police; and (3) manage the CONSEQUENCES (acute + long-term complications, specialist care, esp. deinfibulation for Type 3).
The single most examined point is the mandatory reporting duty + its precise scope (known cases, under-18s only). Reflex: FGM identified/disclosed in a girl UNDER 18 → mandatory report to police (call 101); a girl AT RISK → safeguarding referral; an adult over 18 → sensitive care ± safeguarding for others. Culturally-rooted (parts of Africa/Middle East/Asia); performed on girls (often young); no religious basis.
The Decisive Fork — The WHO Classification (Types 1–4)
TypeDescription

Type 2 (Excision)partial or total removal of the clitoris + LABIA MINORA, ± excision of the labia majora
Type 3 (Infibulation)NARROWING of the vaginal orifice with a covering SEAL — cutting + appositioning the labia, ± excision of the clitoris (the most extensive)
Type 4ALL other harmful procedures — pricking, piercing, incising, scraping, cauterisation
The rule: Type 1 = clitoris (clitoridectomy); Type 2 = clitoris + labia minora (excision); Type 3 = narrowing/sealing the vaginal orifice (INFIBULATION — most extensive); Type 4 = all other (prick/pierce/scrape/cauterise). Infibulation (Type 3) causes the most obstetric/gynaecological problems (obstructed flow/intercourse/delivery) → may need DEINFIBULATION (surgical opening).
Complications
⚡ Acute (at the time)
  • Severe pain, HAEMORRHAGE, shock
  • Infection (incl. tetanus, HIV/hepatitis from shared instruments)
  • Urinary retention, genital tissue injury, DEATH
⏳ Long-term
  • Urinary: recurrent UTIs, dysuria, obstruction/retention
  • Menstrual/gynae: dysmenorrhoea, haematocolpos, difficult examinations
  • Sexual: dyspareunia, reduced function
  • Obstetric: obstructed labour, perineal tears, PPH, need for deinfibulation
  • Psychological: PTSD, anxiety, depression
The rule: FGM complications = acute (haemorrhage/infection/death) + long-term (recurrent UTIs, dyspareunia, obstetric complications, psychological trauma).
The UK Legal Framework (Guideline-Verified)
FGM is ILLEGAL in the UK — the FEMALE GENITAL MUTILATION ACT 2003 (amended by the Serious Crime Act 2015) makes it a criminal offence to perform FGM, assist/arrange it, or fail to protect a girl from it. It is illegal to take a girl abroad (or arrange) for FGM (extraterritorial). Maximum penalty = 14 years' imprisonment; there is a separate offence of failing to protect a girl (under 16) from FGM.
🛡️ FGM Protection Order (FGMPO)
  • A civil court order to protect a girl AT RISK
  • e.g. removing/surrendering her passport to prevent her being taken abroad
🔒 Victim anonymity
  • Lifelong anonymity for FGM survivors
The rule: FGM Act 2003 (+ Serious Crime Act 2015) → performing/arranging/failing-to-protect is illegal (max 14 years); FGM Protection Orders protect girls at risk; victim anonymity; taking abroad for FGM is illegal.
The MANDATORY REPORTING DUTY (The Key Exam Point)
The mandatory reporting duty (FGM Act 2003 section 5B, added by the Serious Crime Act 2015; in force 31 Oct 2015):

The critical LIMITS of the duty (commonly tested): it applies ONLY to girls UNDER 18; it does NOT apply to “at risk”/“suspected” cases (→ normal SAFEGUARDING referral to children's services, NOT the police duty); it does NOT apply if an adult (≥18) discloses FGM she had as a child (→ local safeguarding, consider risk to other girls); and a disclosure by a PARENT/relative (not the girl herself) does NOT trigger the mandatory duty (though safeguarding still applies).
The rule: KNOWN FGM (disclosed by, or visibly identified in, a girl UNDER 18) → MANDATORY report to POLICE (101); AT RISK / SUSPECTED / adult → SAFEGUARDING referral (children's services), NOT the mandatory police duty.

🤝 Approach
  • Sensitive, non-judgemental, culturally-aware care
  • Use interpreters (not family); document carefully
  • Psychological support for trauma/PTSD
🩺 Practical

  • Specialist FGM services; DEINFIBULATION (opening Type 3) — antenatally, in labour, or non-pregnant

OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Androgen Insen:
Definition & The Core Concept

Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS, “testicular feminisation”) = an X-LINKED RECESSIVE disorder of end-organ RESISTANCE to testosterone — a mutation in the ANDROGEN RECEPTOR gene on the X chromosome → a genotypically MALE (46,XY) child develops a FEMALE phenotype. It is a disorder of sex development (DSD).

The core concept — one defect explains everything: the androgen receptor doesn't work. Although the individual is 46,XY with functioning TESTES producing testosterone, the tissues cannot RESPOND to androgens → external genitalia default to the female pattern. Testosterone is still aromatised to OESTROGEN → driving breast development. And the testes still make anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) → which suppresses the Müllerian (female internal) structures (upper vagina, uterus, cervix, fallopian tubes).
The result: female external appearance + breasts, BUT no uterus/ovaries + intra-abdominal testes + primary amenorrhoea. Reflex: a phenotypic female with primary amenorrhoea + absent uterus + scant pubic/axillary hair + inguinal “hernias” (testes) = AIS → karyotype 46,XY. Two forms: COMPLETE (CAIS — fully female phenotype) and PARTIAL (PAIS — ambiguous/undervirilised genitalia).

Oestrogen (aromatised from testosterone)produced + tissues respondbreast development + female habitus
The rule: testosterone HIGH but not sensed (→ female external genitalia); AMH present (→ NO female internal organs); oestrogen from aromatisation (→ breasts) — the three signals explain the whole picture.
Why no ovaries AND no uterus: there are NO ovaries (the gonads are testes — 46,XY) and NO uterus (AMH suppressed the Müllerian ducts) → a blind-ending vagina, no menstruation, and infertility.

  • A key trigger to investigate

  • Scant pubic/axillary hair + a short/blind-ending vagina
Also: absence of uterus, upper vagina, cervix, fallopian tubes, ovaries; breast development occurs (testosterone → oestradiol).
The hair point: little/no pubic + axillary hair — because these are androgen-dependent (and androgens aren't sensed) → a useful discriminator.
The rule: AIS = phenotypic female + PRIMARY AMENORRHOEA + breast development + SCANT pubic/axillary hair + inguinal testes/hernias + NO uterus.

The rule: karyotype 46,XY + high (male-range) testosterone + raised LH + absent uterus/ovaries on imaging + intra-abdominal testes = AIS.

The principle: multidisciplinary (endocrine/gynae/urology/psychology/genetics) + sensitive counselling; sex of rearing (usually female in CAIS); GONADECTOMY (timing now usually DEFERRED to post-puberty); OESTROGEN replacement after gonadectomy; support.

🔪 Gonadectomy — the timing shift
  • Intra-abdominal/undescended testes carry an increased risk of gonadal (germ-cell) MALIGNANCY
  • BUT the pre-pubertal risk is LOW, and retaining the testes allows spontaneous puberty/feminisation (via aromatisation) → gonadectomy is now typically DEFERRED until AFTER puberty (a shared decision, gonads often retained into early adulthood with surveillance)
  • Risk rises with age; modern estimates of frank malignancy are lower than older figures (~1–2%, premalignant change ~6%, almost all post-pubertal)
💊 Oestrogen replacement
  • After gonadectomy → OESTROGEN replacement is essential → maintains secondary sexual characteristics + protects BONE (osteoporosis) and cardiovascular/metabolic health
  • NO progesterone needed — there's no uterus/endometrium to protect
Other: vaginal dilation or surgery if the vagina is short (sexual function); psychological support; genetic counselling (X-linked — implications for relatives); infertility counselling (no uterus/ovaries → cannot carry a pregnancy).

Overview — antepartum haemorrhage & placental disorders
Bleeding from 24 weeks (antepartum haemorrhage, APH) and disorders of placental site/implantation. The two major causes of APH are placenta praevia and placental abruption; vasa praevia and the accreta spectrum are rarer but critical.
The organising principle: is the bleeding painless or painful, and is the uterus soft or tender? Praevia = painless bleeding, soft non-tender uterus (do NOT perform a vaginal exam until praevia is excluded); abruption = painful bleeding, tender “woody” uterus ± fetal distress.

What & Why

Placenta praevia = a placenta lying wholly or partly in the LOWER uterine segment → at or covering the internal cervical os, in the path of delivery. Its hallmark is PAINLESS antepartum haemorrhage in the second half of pregnancy.

The core concept — a problem of placental LOCATION: the placenta implanted low, over/near the cervix. Two consequences: (1) BLEEDING — as the lower segment stretches + the cervix effaces later in pregnancy, the low placenta shears off → PAINLESS, unprovoked vaginal bleeding (soft, non-tender uterus — unlike abruption); and (2) it BLOCKS the exit → vaginal delivery is unsafe if the placenta covers the os → CAESAREAN.
The golden rule: NO digital vaginal examination (can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage) → diagnose by ultrasound; usually found incidentally at the 20-week scan. Reflex: painless vaginal bleeding in later pregnancy + a soft non-tender uterus = placenta praevia → NO vaginal exam → transvaginal ultrasound → caesarean if praevia.

What & Why

Vasa praevia = unprotected FETAL blood vessels running through the placental MEMBRANES, across or near the internal os, below the presenting part — unsupported by placental tissue or the cord's Wharton's jelly. Because they're unprotected, they RUPTURE when the membranes break → fetal exsanguination.

The core concept — the third “praevia”, but a FETAL (not maternal) catastrophe. In praevia/abruption the bleeding is maternal; in vasa praevia it is FETAL — and because the fetal blood volume is tiny (~80–100 ml/kg), even a small bleed can rapidly exsanguinate + kill the fetus. When the membranes rupture (spontaneously or at amniotomy), the naked vessels tear → painless vaginal bleeding + immediate fetal collapse (bradycardia/death).
The single most important fact: diagnosed ANTENATALLY → planned caesarean → survival >95%; presents acutely at membrane rupture → fetal mortality ~60%. Management = antenatal DETECTION + elective caesarean BEFORE labour. Reflex: painless vaginal bleeding + fetal bradycardia immediately after the membranes rupture = vasa praevia → emergency caesarean. Classic triad: membrane rupture + painless bleeding + fetal bradycardia.

What & Why

Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) = abnormally ADHERENT or INVASIVE placentation — the placenta attaches through/into the myometrium because of a DEFECTIVE DECIDUA BASALIS → it fails to separate at delivery → risk of catastrophic postpartum haemorrhage. A spectrum by depth: accreta → increta → percreta.

The core concept — a damaged/absent decidua basalis (the normal cleavage plane), usually at a previous uterine scar (caesarean). Normally the placenta separates cleanly along this decidual layer; in PAS there's no cleavage plane → the placenta is anchored into (or through) the myometrium → in the third stage it won't detach → torrential haemorrhage.
Outcomes are transformed by ANTENATAL diagnosis → a planned specialist-MDT caesarean (usually with hysterectomy). Two key facts: (1) strongly linked to PREVIOUS CAESAREAN + PLACENTA PRAEVIA, and (2) management is usually CAESAREAN + HYSTERECTOMY with the placenta LEFT IN SITU (do NOT forcibly remove it). Reflex: placenta praevia + previous caesarean → screen for accreta antenatally → plan a specialist caesarean-hysterectomy.

Ectopic pregnancy = implantation OUTSIDE the uterine cavity — most commonly the FALLOPIAN TUBE (~95%, esp. ampulla). What & Why

Gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) = a spectrum from abnormal proliferation of placental TROPHOBLAST tissue. It ranges from the benign/premalignant MOLAR PREGNANCIES (complete + partial hydatidiform moles) through to the MALIGNANT forms — “gestational trophoblastic NEOPLASIA (GTN)” (invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, PSTT). Hallmark: very high hCG + first-trimester bleeding + a “grape-like/snowstorm” uterus.

The core concept — the trophoblast proliferates out of control, with little/no normal fetal development. Because trophoblast makes hCG, the defining feature is a markedly ELEVATED hCG → which explains most of the picture: exaggerated pregnancy symptoms (severe hyperemesis), early pre-eclampsia, and (because hCG structurally resembles TSH) hyperthyroidism. Threads: recognise it → urgent EVACUATION + histology → register + serial hCG FOLLOW-UP (a mole can progress to GTN needing chemotherapy).
Good news: GTN is the most CURABLE gynaecological malignancy (>90–95% cure, chemo-sensitive). Reflex: first-trimester bleeding + uterus large for dates + very high hCG + snowstorm scan = molar pregnancy → evacuate + register + hCG follow-up.

🔎 Features
  • PAINLESS bleeding in the 1st/early-2nd trimester
  • EXAGGERATED pregnancy symptoms — e.g. HYPEREMESIS
  • Uterus VERY LARGE for dates
  • VERY HIGH hCG; HTN + HYPERTHYROIDISM may be seen (hCG mimics TSH); ± “grape-like” vesicles, theca lutein cysts

  • Very high serum hCG (diagnosis + monitoring)

The rule: painless first/early-2nd-trimester bleeding + uterus large for dates + VERY high hCG + hyperemesis ± early pre-eclampsia/hyperthyroidism → ultrasound (SNOWSTORM) → DEFINITIVE diagnosis on HISTOLOGY.

The principle: urgent EVACUATION + histology → REGISTER with a specialist GTD centre → serial hCG FOLLOW-UP → chemotherapy if it progresses to GTN; avoid pregnancy during follow-up.
🔧 Evacuation
  • Urgent uterine EVACUATION — SUCTION CURETTAGE is the method of choice for a COMPLETE mole (partial mole with fetal parts may need medical evacuation)
  • Products MUST go for HISTOLOGICAL examination
  • Anti-D if Rhesus-negative; avoid oxytocics before evacuation completes (embolisation risk)
📋 Register + follow-up
  • REGISTER with a specialist GTD centre (UK standard of care)
  • Serial hCG monitoring until normal → detects persistent/malignant disease
  • Effective contraception to avoid pregnancy during follow-up (a new pregnancy's hCG confuses monitoring)

Overview — hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Hypertension arising in pregnancy — gestational hypertension and the multisystem disorder pre-eclampsia (→ eclampsia). A major cause of maternal and fetal morbidity.
The organising principle: timing + proteinuria + organ features. New hypertension after 20 weeks: without proteinuria/organ involvement = gestational HTN; with proteinuria or organ dysfunction = pre-eclampsia; with seizures = eclampsia.

Give magnesium sulfate for eclampsia/severe pre-eclampsia (seizure treatment & prevention). Definitive treatment of pre-eclampsia is delivery. Watch for HELLP (haemolysis, ↑LFTs, low platelets).
What & Why

Pre-eclampsia = a multisystem disorder defined by NEW hypertension + end-organ dysfunction (classically proteinuria) after 20 weeks. A leading cause of maternal + fetal death worldwide, yet largely preventable (aspirin) and treatable (the cure is delivery).

The unifying concept — the PLACENTA is the problem. Abnormal spiral-artery remodelling → a poorly perfused, ischaemic placenta → release of anti-angiogenic factors → widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction → hypertension, proteinuria (leaky glomeruli), oedema, multi-organ complications. This is why delivering the placenta is definitively curative.
Eclampsia = pre-eclampsia + a tonic-clonic seizure — the feared endpoint. Seizures can occur antenatally, intrapartum, or POSTNATALLY (a classic trap — pre-eclampsia doesn't end at delivery).

Diagnosis (NICE NG133 — Guideline-Verified)

Hypertension ≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions after 20 weeks, PLUS at least one of:

🧪 Proteinuria / organ dysfunction
  • Proteinuria — urine protein:creatinine ratio (PCR) ≥30 mg/mmol (or ACR ≥8; don't use a first-morning void to quantify)
  • Renal (raised creatinine), hepatic (raised transaminases ± RUQ/epigastric pain)
  • Neurological (visual disturbance, severe headache, clonus)
  • Haematological (thrombocytopenia, DIC, haemolysis)
👶 Uteroplacental
  • Fetal growth restriction
PLGF-based testing (placental growth factor), between 20 and 36⁺⁶ weeks, helps RULE OUT pre-eclampsia in suspected disease (low PLGF supports it — the anti-angiogenic marker).

🔴 High-risk (any ONE → aspirin)
  • Hypertensive disease in a previous pregnancy
  • Chronic hypertension
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Diabetes (type 1 or 2)
  • Autoimmune disease (SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome)
🟠 Moderate-risk (TWO+ → aspirin)
  • First pregnancy (nulliparity)
  • Age ≥40
  • BMI ≥35
  • Family history of pre-eclampsia
  • Multiple pregnancy
  • Pregnancy interval >10 years
Prophylaxis: aspirin 75–150 mg once daily from 12 weeks until birth (many protocols use 150 mg at night; start before 16 weeks for maximal effect).
Investigations (Monitoring the Diagnosed Patient)
🔬 Surveillance
  • BP + urine PCR/dipstick (serial)
  • Bloods: FBC (falling platelets = worrying), U&Es/creatinine, LFTs (transaminases), coagulation/LDH/haptoglobin/blood film if HELLP suspected
  • PLGF-based testing
  • Fetal: growth-scan ultrasound, umbilical artery Doppler, CTG
Management
📷 Image placeholder — Magnesium sulfate — IV loading then maintenance infusion; monitor reflexes/respiratory rate/urine output; absent deep-tendon reflexes = first sign of toxicity → IV calcium gluconate
The definitive treatment is DELIVERY of the fetus + placenta. Everything else temporises to allow fetal maturity while keeping the mother safe.
💊 Antihypertensives
  • 1st line: LABETALOL (oral, or IV in severe disease)
  • 2nd line: NIFEDIPINE (if labetalol unsuitable — e.g. asthma)
  • 3rd line: METHYLDOPA
  • Target BP ≤135/85
  • ACE inhibitors/ARBs CONTRAINDICATED (fetal renal damage, oligohydramnios) — classic trap
⚡ Seizures — MAGNESIUM SULFATE
  • Treats AND prevents eclamptic seizures (drug of choice, superior to diazepam/phenytoin)
  • Given in severe pre-eclampsia + eclampsia (IV loading → maintenance infusion)
  • Toxicity: loss of deep tendon reflexes (first sign) → respiratory depression → cardiac arrest
  • Antidote = IV calcium gluconate; monitor reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output
Timing of birth: corticosteroids (fetal lung maturity) if preterm delivery anticipated; deliver by gestation + severity; severe/uncontrolled disease → birth within 24–48h once the mother is stabilised. Continue BP monitoring + treatment POSTNATALLY — disease + seizures can worsen after delivery.
Managing an eclamptic seizure: ABCDE, protect the airway, IV magnesium sulfate (loading + maintenance), control BP (IV labetalol/hydralazine), then expedite delivery once the mother is stabilised.
HELLP Syndrome — the Key Complication
A severe variant/complication: Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets. Presents with RUQ/epigastric pain, nausea, malaise ± the pre-eclampsia picture. Serious — risk of liver haematoma/rupture + DIC. Management: stabilise + deliver.

HELLP → deliver. PLGF testing helps rule out pre-eclampsia (20–36⁺⁶ weeks). Don't relax after delivery — monitor BP postnatally.
What & Why

Gestational hypertension (pregnancy-induced hypertension) = new hypertension after 20 weeks WITHOUT proteinuria or organ dysfunction (which would make it pre-eclampsia).

The core idea — it is pre-eclampsia's ANTECHAMBER. Up to a quarter of women with gestational hypertension go on to develop pre-eclampsia → the condition is defined as much by what you watch for as by what it is.

Exam framing: high BP first detected at 28 weeks, dipstick clear, bloods normal → gestational hypertension. Same BP but with proteinuria or deranged LFTs/platelets → it has become pre-eclampsia. High BP already present at booking (before 20 weeks) → chronic hypertension.
Diagnosis (NICE NG133 — Guideline-Verified)
📋 Criteria
  • New hypertension ≥140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks, on two occasions
  • NO proteinuria (urine PCR <30 mg/mmol) + NO maternal organ / uteroplacental dysfunction
  • Severity graded as for pre-eclampsia: mild-moderate up to <160/110; severe ≥160/110
Investigations
The whole point is surveillance for progression to pre-eclampsia: BP monitoring (frequency scaled to severity); urine dipstick/PCR at each visit — the key test to catch the transition; bloods (FBC, U&Es, LFTs) as indicated; PLGF-based testing if pre-eclampsia is suspected (20–36⁺⁶ weeks); fetal monitoring (growth scans/Doppler) if concern arises.
Management (NICE NG133 — Guideline-Verified)
💊 Antihypertensive ladder (same as pre-eclampsia)
  • 1st line: LABETALOL
  • 2nd line: NIFEDIPINE (if labetalol unsuitable, e.g. asthma)
  • 3rd line: METHYLDOPA
  • Target BP ≤135/85
  • ACE inhibitors/ARBs contraindicated (fetal renal damage)
📅 Timing + postnatal
  • Aim to continue to term where BP is controlled + no complications
  • Deliver earlier if it progresses to pre-eclampsia or BP is uncontrolled
  • Postnatal: BP usually normalises but must be monitored + treatment weaned
  • Flags a higher lifetime risk of chronic hypertension + cardiovascular disease → follow-up
Aspirin note: a hypertensive disorder in a previous pregnancy is itself a high-risk factor → aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks in any subsequent pregnancy.

Overview — medical disorders in pregnancy
Pre-existing or pregnancy-induced medical conditions that complicate pregnancy and need specific monitoring and treatment (“maternal medicine”).
The organising principle: pregnancy alters physiology and drug safety. Many conditions need screening (e.g. GDM), prophylaxis (VTE) or specific treatment, always weighing maternal and fetal wellbeing.

What & Why

Gestational diabetes (GDM) = glucose intolerance first recognised in pregnancy — driven by the insulin resistance that placental hormones (human placental lactogen, cortisol, progesterone) create to divert glucose to the fetus. Maternal hyperglycaemia crosses the placenta → macrosomia → shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycaemia. A red flag for future type 2 diabetes.

The Decisive Fork — Fasting Glucose at Diagnosis (NICE NG3)

Diagnosis — the 75g OGTT (“5678”): fasting ≥5.6 mmol/L OR 2-hour ≥7.8 mmol/L — either value alone diagnoses. Screen: previous GDM → OGTT ASAP after booking + repeat 24–28 wks; any other risk factor → OGTT at 24–28 weeks.
Risk factors: BMI >30, previous macrosomic baby (≥4.5 kg), previous GDM, first-degree relative with diabetes, high-prevalence ethnicity (South Asian, Black Caribbean, Middle Eastern). Glycosuria trap: a trace of glucose on urine dip is NORMAL in pregnancy (↑GFR + reduced tubular reabsorption) — do NOT screen with urinalysis/fasting glucose/HbA1c; use the OGTT.
Management & Targets
💊 Glucose-lowering ladder
  • Newly diagnosed → joint diabetes/antenatal clinic within 1 week; teach capillary self-monitoring
  • Diet + exercise first (fasting <7, no complications) — review targets in 1–2 weeks
  • Metformin if targets not met
  • Insulin if metformin insufficient, or first-line if fasting ≥7 (or 6.0–6.9 + complications)
🎯 Glucose targets
  • Fasting: <5.3 mmol/L
  • 1 hour post-meal: <7.8
  • 2 hours post-meal: <6.4
  • Keep >4 mmol/L (avoid hypos) if on insulin
Fetal surveillance + delivery: growth scans for macrosomia/polyhydramnios; timed delivery by ~40–41 weeks (elective birth offered no later than 40⁺⁶), earlier if on treatment/complications.
Postnatal (easily forgotten): STOP all glucose-lowering treatment immediately after birth (GDM resolves with the placenta); monitor the neonate for hypoglycaemia; maternal fasting glucose/HbA1c at 6–13 weeks postnatally, then annual HbA1c (high future type 2 diabetes risk).

What & Why

Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) (obstetric cholestasis) = a liver disorder unique to pregnancy — bile acids accumulate in the maternal circulation causing intense itch, typically in the 3rd trimester, resolving after delivery. At high bile-acid levels it raises stillbirth risk → management centres on measuring bile acids + timing delivery.

Mechanism: impaired bile flow → raised serum bile acids → thought to cross to the fetus + at high concentrations trigger fetal cardiac arrhythmia / placental vasospasm → sudden stillbirth. The bile-acid level, not the symptoms, drives risk.

Features & Investigations
🔎 Clinical features
  • Pruritus — the cardinal, often ONLY feature — classically worse on palms + soles, worse at night; NO rash (excoriations only)
  • Raised bilirubin in ~90%; clinical jaundice in only ~20%
  • Dark urine, pale stools, RUQ discomfort, fatigue (variable)
🧪 Investigations
  • Serum bile acids — key diagnostic + prognostic test
  • LFTs — transaminases (ALT/AST) often raised; use pregnancy-adjusted ranges (ALP rises physiologically → not useful)
  • Diagnosis of exclusion — rule out viral hepatitis, liver autoantibodies, liver ultrasound, pre-eclampsia/HELLP
  • Confirmed retrospectively by resolution postnatally
Management (RCOG GTG43 2022 — Guideline-Verified)
UDCA is NOT routinely recommended — the PITCHES RCT showed it does not prevent stillbirth + has only limited/insignificant benefit on itch. The old “give everyone UDCA” teaching is superseded; there is no treatment that reliably improves outcome or lowers bile acids (UDCA may be considered on an individual basis).
💧 Supportive
  • Topical emollients (menthol in aqueous cream) — safe, may soothe
  • Chlorphenamine (sedating antihistamine) — helps sleep, limited effect on itch
  • Water-soluble vitamin K only if prolonged clotting / severe cholestasis (impaired fat-soluble vitamin absorption → bleeding risk)
📅 Timing of birth (bile-acid-stratified)
  • ≥100 (severe): planned birth ~35–36 weeks
  • 40–99 (moderate): ~38–39 weeks
  • <40 (mild): ~40 weeks
  • Co-existing GDM/pre-eclampsia/multiple pregnancy → earlier
Monitoring: serial bile acids + LFTs guide delivery timing; CTG is offered but cannot reliably predict/prevent the sudden stillbirth. Postnatal: confirm resolution (LFT/bile-acid check ~4+ weeks); high recurrence (~45–90%); small increased lifetime hepatobiliary risk (gallstones).

Pruritus (palms/soles, NO rash) + raised bile acids in the 3rd trimester, resolving after birth.

Itch with NO rash is the main/only symptom.

Bile-acid-stratified: ~35–36 wk if ≥100; ~38–39 wk if 40–99; ~40 wk if <40 — not a flat 37–38 weeks.

What & Why

VTE (DVT + pulmonary embolism, PE) is a leading direct cause of maternal death — pregnancy is a major prothrombotic state. Diagnosis deliberately differs from the non-pregnant pathway (no D-dimer or Wells scoring), and prevention hinges on the RCOG risk-scoring tool.

Virchow's triad, all three arms: hypercoagulability (oestrogen ↑clotting factors, ↓protein S), stasis (uterine venous compression), endothelial injury (at delivery). Risk is highest in the third trimester and the puerperium (first 6 weeks — greatest daily risk of all).
Prevention — Risk Scoring & Prophylaxis (RCOG GTG37a)
Every woman is risk-assessed at booking, on any admission, intrapartum + postnatally (risk is dynamic). RCOG uses a cumulative risk-factor score. Risk factors: age >35, BMI >30, parity ≥3, smoker, gross varicose veins, current pre-eclampsia, immobility, multiple pregnancy, IVF, family history of unprovoked VTE, thrombophilia, medical comorbidities (SLE, IBD, cancer), transient factors (hyperemesis/dehydration, OHSS, surgery, long-haul travel).

Agent: LMWH (enoxaparin) — doesn't cross the placenta. DOACs + warfarin contraindicated (warfarin teratogenic — fetal warfarin syndrome). Monitor anti-Xa only at body-weight extremes (<50 or ≥90 kg) or renal impairment — not routinely. Caesarean + additional risk factors (or emergency caesarean) → postnatal LMWH. Mechanical: anti-embolism stockings, mobilisation, hydration.
Acute VTE — Diagnosis & Treatment (RCOG GTG37b)
🩻 Diagnosis (pregnancy changes the rules)
  • D-dimer NOT used (rises physiologically) + Wells score NOT validated
  • Suspected DVT: compression duplex ultrasound (more often left-sided/iliofemoral); if negative but suspicious, repeat days 3 + 7
  • Suspected PE: ECG + CXR first; if DVT signs → leg ultrasound first (avoids radiation); else V/Q scan or CTPA (guided by CXR)
💉 Treatment
  • Start treatment-dose LMWH immediately on suspicion — don't wait for imaging
  • LMWH = treatment of choice; continue ≥3 months AND until ≥6 weeks postnatal (whichever longer)
  • Do NOT delay for a thrombophilia screen
  • Massive/life-threatening PE → IV unfractionated heparin or thrombolysis; stop LMWH at labour onset / before planned delivery (regional-anaesthesia timing)

Leading direct cause of maternal death; risk highest in the 3rd trimester + puerperium; pregnancy = Virchow's triad in full.

What & Why

Hyperemesis gravidarum (HG) = the severe end of nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NVP) — vomiting causing weight loss, dehydration + electrolyte disturbance. NVP is near-universal + benign; HG is the ~0.3–3.6% who become genuinely unwell. A leading cause of early-pregnancy admission with a specific complication (Wernicke's) to prevent.

Mechanism: driven by elevated β-hCG → worse in high-β-hCG states (multiple pregnancy, molar/trophoblastic disease). β-hCG mimics TSH → severe HG can cause transient biochemical hyperthyroidism.
The Decisive Fork — NVP vs True HG
🔺 RCOG diagnostic triad for HG
  • ≥5% pre-pregnancy weight loss
  • Dehydration
  • Electrolyte imbalance
  • Onset before 16 weeks (part of the NVP definition)
📊 PUQE severity score
  • Scores nausea duration + vomiting + retching over 24h
  • ≤6 mild · 7–12 moderate · 13–15 severe
  • (HELP tool = newer validated alternative)
Key differential: vomiting starting after ~11–16 weeks, or with abdominal pain/fever/dysuria → search for another cause (UTI, gastroenteritis, molar pregnancy, thyroid/liver disease) — HG is partly a diagnosis of exclusion. Risk factors (mostly “more β-hCG”): multiple pregnancy, molar disease, nulliparity, obesity, personal/family history of HG, female fetus.
Investigations
Weight (vs pre-pregnancy); MSU to exclude UTI; U&Es (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia), FBC (haemoconcentration); TFTs/LFTs if indicated; ultrasound to confirm a viable intrauterine pregnancy + exclude multiple/molar pregnancy.
Update (RCOG GTG69 2024, Grade A): ketonuria is NOT an indicator of dehydration + should NOT be used to assess severity. Older teaching leaning on ketones is rejected — use the PUQE score, weight loss, clinical dehydration + electrolytes instead.
Management
💊 Antiemetics — stepwise
  • 1st-line: antihistamines (cyclizine/promethazine), phenothiazines (prochlorperazine/chlorpromazine), doxylamine/pyridoxine (Xonvea)
  • 2nd-line: ondansetron (counsel on small cleft-palate risk in 1st trimester — benefit outweighs it), metoclopramide (max 5 days — extrapyramidal/oculogyric crisis) or domperidone
  • Combination therapy if single agent fails; corticosteroids for refractory HG
  • Conservative: rest, small bland meals, ginger, P6 acupressure
💧 IV fluids + thiamine
  • Normal saline + potassium chloride to correct dehydration/hypokalaemia
  • NO glucose/dextrose fluids — precipitates Wernicke's in a thiamine-deficient woman
  • THIAMINE to ALL admitted with prolonged vomiting (oral 100 mg TDS or IV Pabrinex) BEFORE any dextrose → prevents Wernicke's (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia)
  • VTE prophylaxis (LMWH) during admission (dehydration + immobility)
Setting: mild → community oral antiemetics; ambulatory day-care if community fails + PUQE <13; admit if can't tolerate oral fluids/antiemetics, continued vomiting + weight loss, PUQE ≥13, or comorbidity. Add PPI/H2 antagonist for reflux + mental-health support.

What it is
Severe NVP: ≥5% weight loss + dehydration + electrolyte imbalance; onset <16 weeks; driven by β-hCG → worse in multiple/molar → always ultrasound.

What & Why

Substance use in pregnancy (alcohol, tobacco, illicit/prescribed drugs) is among the commonest preventable causes of fetal harm, clustering with social vulnerability (safeguarding lens). Recurring principle: support + substitution, not judgement or abrupt withdrawal — a judged woman disengages from antenatal care.

Two substances break the “just stop” rule because abrupt cessation is itself dangerous: opioids and alcohol/benzodiazepines (withdrawal risk).

Alcohol & Tobacco
🍷 Alcohol
  • UK guidance: avoid completely — no safe threshold; risk dose-related
  • Fetal Alcohol Syndrome: smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, small palpebral fissures (the facial triad) + growth restriction + CNS/neurodevelopmental (microcephaly, learning disability)
  • Heavy/dependent drinkers need supported detox (abrupt withdrawal → seizures/delirium tremens; thiamine cover)
🚬 Tobacco
  • CO + nicotine → chronic fetal hypoxia + vasoconstriction → growth restriction (low birth weight), abruption, praevia, preterm birth/PPROM, miscarriage/stillbirth, SIDS
  • Ask + CO breath test at booking; refer all smokers to Stop Smoking Services (opt-out)
  • NRT if behavioural support fails (safer than smoking); varenicline + bupropion avoided in pregnancy
Opioids, Stimulants & General Principles
💉 Opioids
  • Do NOT attempt abrupt withdrawal (fetal distress, miscarriage, preterm birth)
  • Opioid substitution — methadone or buprenorphine, maintained throughout via a specialist drug service
  • Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome: high-pitched cry, jitteriness, tremors, poor feeding, sweating, diarrhoea, seizures (CNS + GI + autonomic) → Finnegan scoring, supportive care, weaning oral morphine if severe (also with benzodiazepines)
⚕️ Stimulants + principles
  • Cocaine → placental abruption (vasoconstriction), growth restriction, maternal hypertension/stroke/MI; no substitution — supportive/safeguarding
  • Cannabis → growth restriction + neurodevelopmental effects
  • General: non-judgemental engagement, MDT + safeguarding (“complex social factors”), screen for blood-borne viruses (hep B/C, HIV) in injecting users, enhanced growth surveillance; breastfeeding encouraged on stable methadone/buprenorphine

Overarching
Non-judgemental engagement + MDT + safeguarding keeps women in care; injecting use → screen HIV/hep B/hep C.
What & Why

Rhesus (RhD) disease = haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN) — an RhD-negative mother sensitised to the RhD antigen on her RhD-positive baby's red cells; in a later pregnancy her anti-D antibodies cross the placenta + haemolyse a subsequent RhD-positive fetus. Now almost entirely preventable with anti-D prophylaxis.

The two-hit logic: ~15% of the UK is RhD-negative. First exposure (a sensitising event — fetal RhD+ cells enter maternal circulation) → primary immune response → maternal anti-D IgG (current baby usually unaffected). Subsequent RhD+ pregnancy → anti-D IgG crosses the placenta → haemolyses fetal red cells → HDFN. This is why the first affected pregnancy is usually the second.
The Decisive Fork — Sensitised or Not?
Not yet sensitisedAlready sensitised
GoalPREVENT sensitisationMONITOR & TREAT the affected fetus
ToolAnti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxisAntibody titres, MCA Doppler, fetal transfusion
Key pointAnti-D works only before sensitisationAnti-D is useless once sensitised
Anti-D cannot reverse existing sensitisation — once a woman has made her own anti-D antibodies, giving more is pointless. Prophylaxis is purely preventive.
Antenatal Testing & Prevention
🩸 Antenatal testing
  • Booking bloods: ABO group, RhD status, red-cell antibody screen (all women)
  • Repeat antibody screen at ~28 weeks
  • Fetal RHD genotyping (cell-free fetal DNA) from ~11–16 wks — non-invasive; if fetus RhD-negative, anti-D is unnecessary (spares ~40%) — NICE DG25
💉 Anti-D prophylaxis (RAADP)
  • Two-dose: anti-D at 28 + 34 weeks (500 IU each), OR single-dose: 1500 IU once at 28–30 weeks
  • Works by “mopping up” fetal RhD+ cells before the immune system reacts (passive immunisation)
  • Postnatal: if the baby is RhD-positive → anti-D within 72h of delivery
Anti-D after a sensitising event: give ASAP, within 72 hours. Dose: 250 IU before 20 weeks; ≥500 IU from 20 weeks (guided by a Kleihauer test for larger bleeds). Sensitising events: delivery of an RhD+ infant, any termination, miscarriage >12 weeks (or any surgically managed), ectopic, ECV, antepartum haemorrhage, invasive procedures (amniocentesis, CVS, fetal blood sampling), abdominal trauma.
Key Tests & HDFN Management
🔬 Key tests
  • Cord blood (every baby of an RhD-neg mother): FBC, blood group, direct Coombs test (DAT) — positive = maternal antibodies bound to baby's cells
  • Kleihauer test: acid added to maternal blood — adult HbA is eluted, fetal HbF-containing cells resist + stay visible → quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage → sizes the anti-D dose (≥20 wks/large bleeds)
🚨 Once sensitised — HDFN
  • Serial maternal antibody titres
  • MCA Doppler — raised peak systolic velocity = fetal anaemia (non-invasive)
  • Intrauterine (fetal) blood transfusion for significant anaemia
  • Neonate: phototherapy, exchange transfusion, IVIG; severe → hydrops fetalis. Other antibodies (anti-Kell, anti-c) also cause HDFN (Kell suppresses erythropoiesis)
Exam Pearls
Mechanism
RhD-neg mother + RhD-pos fetus → sensitisation → anti-D IgG → haemolysis in the NEXT RhD-pos pregnancy. First pregnancy usually spared.
Anti-D
Prevents sensitisation; does NOTHING once already sensitised.
RAADP
28 & 34 weeks (500 IU each) OR a single 1500 IU dose at 28–30 weeks.
Sensitising event
Anti-D within 72 hours (250 IU <20 wks; ≥500 IU from 20 wks + Kleihauer). Events: delivery, TOP, miscarriage >12 wks, ectopic, ECV, APH, amnio/CVS/fetal blood sampling, abdominal trauma.
Tests
Kleihauer: acid elutes adult HbA, fetal HbF resists → quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage. Direct Coombs (DAT) on cord blood confirms antibody-coated fetal cells. Fetal RHD genotyping (cffDNA) lets you skip anti-D if fetus RhD-negative.
Sensitised
MCA Doppler + intrauterine transfusion; severe → hydrops fetalis.
OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Malpresentatio:
Overview — malpresentation & malposition
Abnormalities of fetal presentation or lie affecting the mode of delivery — most importantly breech presentation and transverse/oblique lie.
The organising principle: determine presentation/lie near term; offer ECV where appropriate. Unstable/transverse lie and breech carry cord-prolapse and delivery risks.
ConditionNote
Breech presentationbuttocks/feet first; offer ECV ~37 wks; planned C-section often chosen; types (frank/complete/footling)
Transverse/abnormal liefetus lies across the uterus; cannot deliver vaginally; cord-prolapse risk; ECV or C-section
Transverse lie with ruptured membranes → high cord-prolapse risk (obstetric emergency). Confirm presentation before labour.
What & Why

Breech presentation = the fetus lies with its buttocks or feet (caudal end) presenting to the pelvis rather than the head — a malpresentation. Complicates ~3–4% of term deliveries; breech babies have worse outcomes than cephalic babies regardless of delivery mode.

Common early, rare at term: the fetus usually turns spontaneously to cephalic as the third trimester progresses → intervention is deliberately timed late, giving nature a chance first. Management pathway: try to turn it (ECV) → if that fails, decide how to deliver (caesarean vs vaginal breech).
The Decisive Fork — Which Type of Breech?
📷 Image placeholder — Breech types side by side — frank (extended), complete (flexed) and footling; hip/knee flexion pattern and which part presents
TypePositionNote
Frank (extended)Hips flexed, knees extended (legs straight up, feet by head)Most common type
Complete (flexed)Hips and knees both flexed (sitting cross-legged)—
FootlingOne/both feet present first, buttocks higherHighest cord-prolapse risk; a contraindication to vaginal breech birth
Natural history: ~25% of pregnancies are breech at 28 weeks, but only ~3–4% at term — most perform a ~180° turn to head-down by ~36 weeks. (A 360° turn would return it to breech.)
Risk Factors & Diagnosis
Risk factors (anything preventing turning/engagement)
  • Uterine abnormalities (malformations, fibroids); placenta praevia
  • Polyhydramnios or oligohydramnios
  • Fetal abnormality (CNS malformation, chromosomal disorders)
  • Prematurity (breech commoner earlier); multiple pregnancy; nulliparity
🔎 Diagnosis
  • Abdominal palpation — hard ballotable head at the fundus; irregular mass in the pelvis; fetal heart higher than expected
  • Confirmed on ultrasound — also assesses type, growth, liquor, placental position
Management
🔄 Step 1–2: watch → offer ECV
  • <36 weeks: watch + wait (most turn spontaneously)
  • Still breech at term → offer External Cephalic Version (ECV) — manual manipulation to cephalic; offered from 36 wks (nulliparous) / 37 wks (multiparous), generally performed at/near term (37+0)
  • Success ~50% (higher in multiparous; <5% revert); reduces caesarean rate
  • Tocolysis (terbutaline) improves success; ~1 in 200 risk of emergency caesarean immediately after → done where caesarean is available
🚫 ECV contraindications
  • Caesarean already indicated for another reason
  • Antepartum haemorrhage in the last 7 days
  • Abnormal CTG; major uterine anomaly
  • Ruptured membranes; placenta praevia
  • Multiple pregnancy (except delivery of a second twin)
Step 3 — still breech (ECV failed/declined/contraindicated) → mode of delivery: planned caesarean reduces perinatal mortality vs planned vaginal breech (Term Breech Trial) + is what most UK women choose (absolute vaginal-breech risk still low ~3/1000). Planned vaginal breech remains an option for selected women with an experienced attendant, but footling breech is a contraindication. Breech babies do worse whatever the mode (the underlying cause partly drives this).
Complications & Exam Pearls
Complications: cord prolapse (esp. footling — presenting part doesn't fill the pelvis); head entrapment, birth trauma, hypoxia in vaginal breech; developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) — breech is a major risk factor → these babies need hip ultrasound screening; increased association with underlying fetal abnormality.
What it is
Buttocks/feet present. ~25% at 28 weeks → only ~3–4% at term (most turn spontaneously).
Three types
Frank (extended, commonest) / Complete (flexed) / Footling. Footling = highest cord-prolapse risk + contraindicates vaginal breech.
Pathway
<36 weeks → watch; term breech → offer ECV (success ~50%, improved by tocolysis, reduces caesarean).
ECV contraindications
Recent APH (<7 days), abnormal CTG, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy, major uterine anomaly, placenta praevia.
Delivery
ECV fails → planned caesarean (safer per Term Breech Trial) vs selected vaginal breech. Breech babies do worse regardless of mode.
Don't forget
Breech → screen for DDH with hip ultrasound. (The natural turn is ~180° to cephalic, not 360°.)
What & Why

Fetal lie = the long axis of the fetus relative to the uterus. Normal = longitudinal. An abnormal lie — transverse (across) or oblique (angled) — is a malpresentation that matters for one dominant reason: you cannot deliver a transverse baby vaginally, and if the membranes rupture the cord (or an arm) can prolapse — an emergency. Rare at term (<0.3%).

The organising principle: an abnormal lie is only a problem at term / in labour — before that it's usually transient + self-correcting. Management is a timeline: watch early → intervene near term → prevent the cord-prolapse catastrophe.
The Decisive Fork — Is It Term Yet?
TimingApproach
<36 weeksNo management — most spontaneously revert to longitudinal. Reassure.
≥36–37 weeks (term)Refer to obstetric team; investigate for a cause; consider ECV; elective admission to guard against cord prolapse; plan delivery.
Types, Terminology & Risk Factors
📷 Image placeholder — Fetal lie compared — longitudinal (normal), transverse (perpendicular) and oblique (angled), showing why a transverse fetus cannot deliver vaginally
🔤 Types
  • Transverse lie — fetal long axis perpendicular; head one lateral side, buttocks the other (scapulo-anterior = commonest; scapulo-posterior)
  • Oblique lie — fetal long axis at an angle (head/buttocks in one iliac fossa)
  • Unstable lie — the lie keeps changing near term (classically multiparous, lax uterus)
Risk factors (“too much room / obstruction”)
  • Multiparity (lax uterus — classic cause of unstable lie); polyhydramnios (fetus floats freely)
  • Prematurity (more room); multiple pregnancy
  • Uterine abnormalities, fibroids, pelvic tumours (distort the cavity)
  • Placenta praevia (blocks engagement); fetal abnormalities
Teaching point: an abnormal lie at term should prompt a search for an underlying cause — especially placenta praevia + fibroids/pelvic mass — it's often not just chance. Diagnosis: abdominal exam (neither head nor buttocks at the fundus/pelvis; fetus felt lying across; presenting part high/absent) → ultrasound confirms the lie + looks for a cause.
Management
Elective admission (the key point): offer admission from ~37 weeks for transverse/oblique/unstable lie — labour or membrane rupture can happen any time, and an abnormal lie with ruptured membranes carries a high cord-prolapse risk → inpatient care allows immediate caesarean. Women in the community must present urgently if contractions start or waters break.
🔄 ECV
  • May be attempted to convert to cephalic (late pregnancy or early labour, if membranes intact)
  • Contraindications as for breech (recent APH, abnormal CTG, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy, major uterine anomaly, placenta praevia)
  • Abnormal/unstable lie tends to revert → ECV alone often insufficient
🏥 Delivery
  • Elective caesarean for persistent transverse/oblique lie, or ECV failure/contraindication/preference
  • Persistent abnormal lie in labour = immediate caesarean (can't deliver transverse vaginally)
  • Ruptured membranes with abnormal lie → expedite delivery by caesarean
  • (“Stabilising induction” — ECV then immediate amniotomy + oxytocin — is a specialist option for selected unstable lie, in theatre with caesarean standby)
Complications & Exam Pearls
Complications: cord prolapse (the major danger — presenting part doesn't fill the pelvis; highest at membrane rupture); PPROM; arm/compound or shoulder presentation if labour progresses; neglected transverse lie → obstructed labour → uterine rupture (the feared end-point); cord/arm prolapse at amniotomy → avoid ARM with a high/mobile presenting part.
Definitions
Lie = fetal long axis vs uterine long axis. Transverse = perpendicular; oblique = angled; unstable = keeps changing. Transverse baby cannot deliver vaginally.
Timeline
<36 weeks → watch (most correct); at term → act.
Elective admission
From ~37 weeks for transverse/oblique/unstable lie — to guard against cord prolapse if membranes rupture.
Find the cause
Abnormal lie at term → look for placenta praevia, fibroids, polyhydramnios, multiparity.
ECV / delivery
ECV can be tried (intact membranes) but often reverts; persistent abnormal lie in labour → immediate caesarean.
Danger
Cord prolapse is the feared complication; neglected transverse lie → obstructed labour → uterine rupture. Unstable lie = classically the multiparous, lax-uterus patient.
OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Preterm Birth:
Overview — preterm birth & PPROM
Birth before 37 weeks and its common precursor, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM). Prematurity is the leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality.
The organising principle: identify preterm labour/PPROM early to deliver interventions that improve neonatal outcome — antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate (neuroprotection), and consideration of tocolysis/in-utero transfer.
ConditionManagement
PPROMconfirm (speculum / IGFBP-1); prophylactic erythromycin; steroids; monitor for chorioamnionitis
Prematurity / preterm laboursteroids; MgSO₄ <34 wks; consider tocolysis + in-utero transfer
Give antenatal corticosteroids (fetal lung maturity) and magnesium sulfate (neuroprotection) in threatened preterm birth; watch for chorioamnionitis in PPROM (deliver if infected).
What & Why

PPROM = spontaneous rupture of the fetal membranes before 37 weeks, before the onset of labour. It’s a major cause of preterm birth (~30–40% of preterm deliveries) and puts the fetus at risk from three directions — prematurity, infection (chorioamnionitis), and cord problems (prolapse, compression from oligohydramnios).

📖 Definitions
  • PROM = rupture before labour, at/after 37 weeks (term)
  • PPROM = rupture before labour, before 37 weeks (preterm — the focus)
  • Prolonged = >24 h between rupture and delivery
⚖️ The core tension
  • The intact sac is a barrier against ascending infection and cushions the cord
  • Once it ruptures preterm you’re caught between delivering (prematurity) and waiting (rising infection/cord risk) — the whole management navigates that trade-off
Clinical Features
  • A gush or trickle of fluid from the vagina (“waters breaking”) — the classic history
  • Persistent feeling of dampness/wetness
  • May have mild irregular contractions/cramps (distinct from established labour)
  • Reduced fetal movements or signs of infection are red flags
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Sterile speculum — pooling of amniotic fluid in the posterior fornix; if no pooling, confirm with IGFBP-1 or PAMG-1 (never a digital exam)
Sterile speculum examination — the key test: look for pooling of amniotic fluid in the posterior vaginal fornix.
Avoid digital vaginal examination — it introduces infection and shortens the latency period.
  • If no pooling seen → biochemical tests on vaginal fluid: PAMG-1 (placental alpha-microglobulin-1, e.g. Amnisure) or IGFBP-1
  • Ultrasound — may show oligohydramnios (supportive, not diagnostic)
  • Monitor for chorioamnionitis: maternal obs, temperature, HR, CRP/WCC, CTG (fetal tachycardia), uterine tenderness, offensive discharge
  • Swabs (including for group B Streptococcus)
Management (RCOG Green-top 73)
Admit and monitor for infection — regular maternal observations to detect chorioamnionitis early.
💊 Prophylactic antibiotics
  • Oral erythromycin 250 mg QDS for 10 days (or until established labour) — reduces chorioamnionitis and delays delivery
  • Avoid co-amoxiclav — associated with neonatal necrotising enterocolitis in this setting
💉 Corticosteroids + magnesium
  • Antenatal corticosteroids — reduce neonatal RDS, IVH, NEC, death; offered up to 34⁺⁶ weeks
  • IV magnesium sulphate (neuroprotection) — reduces cerebral palsy; offered 24⁺⁰–29⁺⁶ weeks (considered to 33⁺⁶) if birth expected within 24 h
Timing of birth — expectant management until 37⁺⁰ weeks is now recommended (better outcomes than early birth) if no contraindications. Update: not 34 weeks — current RCOG favours waiting to 37 if stable. Deliver immediately (any gestation) if chorioamnionitis, fetal distress, cord prolapse, or abruption develops.
Tocolysis is NOT recommended in PPROM (no clear benefit, may mask infection).
Complications
🤰 Maternal
  • Chorioamnionitis (the main one — cause or consequence)
  • Postpartum endometritis, sepsis
👶 Fetal / neonatal
  • Prematurity + sequelae (RDS, IVH, NEC)
  • Cord prolapse (loss of fluid)
  • Cord/limb compression + pulmonary hypoplasia (severe/early oligohydramnios — Potter sequence if very early)
  • Neonatal sepsis
Exam Pearls

PPROM = membrane rupture before labour, before 37 weeks. (PROM = at/after 37; prolonged = >24 h.)
Diagnosis
Sterile speculum → pooling in the posterior fornix. AVOID digital VE (infection risk).
If no pooling
PAMG-1 or IGFBP-1. USS → oligohydramnios (supportive).
Management
Admit + monitor for chorioamnionitis + erythromycin 250 mg QDS 10 days + antenatal corticosteroids + magnesium sulphate (neuroprotection, <30 wks).
Avoid
Co-amoxiclav (neonatal NEC). No tocolysis.
Timing
Expectant management to 37 weeks if stable (update: not 34) — deliver early only if infection/fetal compromise.
Three fetal risks
Prematurity, infection (chorioamnionitis), cord (prolapse/compression). Chorioamnionitis (maternal fever/tachycardia, fetal tachycardia, raised CRP) → deliver now.
What & Why

Preterm birth = delivery before 37⁺⁰ weeks — the leading cause of neonatal death and long-term disability worldwide (the earlier the gestation, the higher the risk). Preterm labour is the process (regular contractions + cervical change before 37 weeks) that leads to it. A huge amount of neonatal outcome hinges on a few time-critical antenatal interventions — corticosteroids and magnesium sulphate — and on correctly identifying who is actually in preterm labour (most symptomatic women are not).

Classification by Gestation
📅 By gestation
  • Extremely preterm: <28 weeks
  • Very preterm: 28–31⁺⁶ weeks
  • Moderate to late preterm: 32–36⁺⁶ weeks
⚖️ By birth weight
  • Low birth weight <2500 g
  • Very low <1500 g
  • Extremely low <1000 g
Preterm Labour — Risk Factors
  • Previous preterm birth (the strongest), previous late miscarriage
  • Multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios (overdistension)
  • PPROM, infection (chorioamnionitis, UTI, BV, group B Streptococcus)
  • Cervical incompetence / previous cervical surgery (LLETZ, cone biopsy)
  • Uterine anomalies, fibroids; antepartum haemorrhage (abruption, praevia)
  • Smoking, low BMI, extremes of maternal age, short inter-pregnancy interval
Diagnosis (NICE NG25)

Clinical: regular painful contractions + cervical change (dilatation/effacement) before 37 weeks. Speculum exam to assess dilatation; if a fetal fibronectin swab is anticipated, take it BEFORE any digital examination.

If diagnosis uncertain (intact membranes)
≤29⁺⁶ weeks
  • If clinical assessment suggests preterm labour → treat (steroids ± tocolysis) without needing further tests
≥30⁺⁰ weeks
  • Offer a diagnostic test for likelihood of birth within 48 h
  • TV ultrasound cervical length — >15 mm = unlikely; ≤15 mm = likely
  • OR fetal fibronectin — positive ≥50 ng/mL = ↑ risk within 7 days; negative = strong reassurance
  • Do NOT use cervical length + fibronectin together
Monitor for infection — CRP, WCC, fetal heart rate (don’t rely on a single CRP).
