📷 Image placeholder — The ~48-hour window — tocolysis (nifedipine) buys time for antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate neuroprotection and in-utero transfer
💉 Corticosteroids
  • Accelerate fetal lung maturity → reduce RDS, IVH, NEC, neonatal death
  • Two doses IM betamethasone/dexamethasone; offered up to 34⁺⁶ weeks
🧠 Magnesium sulphate (neuroprotection)
  • IV magnesium reduces cerebral palsy
  • Birth expected within 24 h, 24⁺⁰–29⁺⁶ weeks (considered to 33⁺⁶)
  • Monitor for toxicity (loss of reflexes, respiratory depression → calcium gluconate)
⏳ Tocolysis
  • Aim: delay ~48 h for steroids to work + in-utero transfer — does NOT improve outcomes alone
  • First-line: nifedipine (CCB), 26⁺⁰–33⁺⁶ weeks, intact membranes
  • Alternative: atosiban (oxytocin receptor antagonist) if nifedipine contraindicated
  • Contraindicated in infection, significant bleeding, fetal compromise
💊 Antibiotics + birth
  • Erythromycin ONLY if membranes ruptured (PPROM) — do NOT give if intact (ORACLE trials)
  • Group B Streptococcus prophylaxis (intrapartum benzylpenicillin) in established preterm labour
  • In-utero transfer; delayed cord clamping (≥60 s) if stable; caesarean for breech 26–36⁺⁶; avoid fetal scalp electrodes <34 wks

Preterm birth = delivery <37 weeks. Extremely (<28), very (28–31⁺⁶), moderate–late (32–36⁺⁶).

≤29⁺⁶ → treat; ≥30 → cervical length (>15 mm unlikely) OR fetal fibronectin (≥50 ng/mL positive). Don’t combine. fFN swab before digital exam.

OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Intrapartum Em:
Overview — intrapartum emergencies
Acute emergencies arising during labour that threaten the fetus and/or mother and demand an immediate, drilled response.
The organising principle: recognise the emergency and act on a rehearsed protocol. Cord prolapse and shoulder dystocia are the classic “call for help now” scenarios.
EmergencyAction
Cord prolapsecord below presenting part after membrane rupture → relieve pressure (elevate presenting part, knee-chest/left lateral), don't handle the cord, emergency C-section
Shoulder dystociaanterior shoulder impacted after head delivers (“turtle” sign) → McRoberts + suprapubic pressure, then internal manoeuvres; brachial-plexus/hypoxia risk
Both are time-critical — summon senior help immediately, don't push the cord back, and follow the shoulder-dystocia manoeuvre sequence (McRoberts first).
What & Why

Umbilical cord prolapse = an obstetric emergency where the umbilical cord descends below the presenting part AFTER the membranes rupture, exposing it to compression + cold. The cord is the baby's lifeline → compression/vasospasm → fetal hypoxia → death or hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy within minutes. Rare (~0.1–0.6%) but a recurring cause of avoidable perinatal death + a mandated labour-ward drill.

Harm is twofold: (1) mechanical compression of the cord between the presenting part + pelvis, and (2) cold/handling-induced arterial vasospasm. Both cut off fetal blood flow → the entire management is about taking pressure off the cord + delivering fast.
The Decisive Fork — Overt vs Occult (and the Defining Condition)
TermDefinitionMembranes
Cord presentationCord lies between presenting part + cervixIntact
Overt cord prolapseCord descends PAST the presenting part (into/through cervix/vagina, may be visible)Ruptured
Occult cord prolapseCord descends alongside (not past) the presenting partRuptured
Cord prolapse requires RUPTURED membranes — with intact membranes the same anatomy is cord presentation (a warning, not the emergency). Exam framing: sudden fetal bradycardia / abnormal CTG immediately after the membranes rupture (esp. after artificial rupture — ARM/amniotomy) → do a vaginal exam to exclude cord prolapse.
Risk Factors & Diagnosis
Risk factors (a poorly-applied presenting part leaves a gap)
  • Abnormal lie/presentation — transverse/unstable lie, breech
  • Prematurity (small presenting part); polyhydramnios (gush sweeps the cord down)
  • Multiple pregnancy (esp. the second twin); high/unengaged presenting part; multiparity
  • Long umbilical cord, low-lying placenta
  • Iatrogenic: ARM with a high presenting part, balloon catheter, external cephalic version
🔎 Diagnosis
  • Palpable cord on vaginal exam, or visible cord at the introitus, after rupture of membranes
  • Fetal heart abnormality — sudden bradycardia or variable decelerations, esp. right after ROM
  • Actively exclude it with a vaginal exam where risk factors exist + after ROM with any CTG abnormality
Management — an Emergency Sequence (RCOG GTG50)
📷 Image placeholder — Cord prolapse — manual elevation of the presenting part + knee–chest position + Foley bladder filling (~500 mL) while preparing for category-1 caesarean
The goal: relieve cord compression + deliver immediately. Call for help (senior obstetric, anaesthetic + neonatal teams; prepare for immediate caesarean).
🙌 Relieve pressure on the cord
  • Manually elevate the presenting part — gloved hand in the vagina, push the presenting part UP off the cord, hold continuously until delivery
  • Position: knee–chest (“all fours”) or exaggerated Sims/left lateral with hips elevated (head-down)
  • Bladder filling — ~500 mL warm saline via a Foley catheter to elevate the presenting part (empty before delivery); useful if delivery/transfer delayed
🚑 Deliver + adjuncts
  • Minimise cord handling (avoid vasospasm); keep warm/moist; do NOT forcibly replace it
  • Stop oxytocin; consider tocolysis (terbutaline) if fetal compromise + delivery delayed
  • Category 1 emergency caesarean (default, deliver within 30 min); instrumental vaginal delivery if fully dilated + imminent
  • Community: knee–chest by phone, call 999, elevate presenting part (midwives carry a Foley for bladder filling)
Transfer tip: knee–chest is unsafe in a moving ambulance — use exaggerated Sims for transfer.
Complications & Exam Pearls
Complications: fetal hypoxia → hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, cerebral palsy, or death (the central danger). Outcomes are worse with prematurity, congenital malformation, and delay in transfer (esp. planned home births).
Definition
Cord past the presenting part with RUPTURED membranes. Intact membranes → cord presentation.
Classic trigger
Sudden fetal bradycardia after ARM/ROM → vaginal exam to exclude cord prolapse.
Manoeuvres
Manually elevate presenting part + knee–chest/left-lateral + fill bladder (500 mL). Minimise cord handling (prevents vasospasm); don't force it back.
Delivery
Category 1 caesarean (or instrumental if fully dilated + imminent). Stop oxytocin; consider tocolysis if delayed.
Risk factors
Breech/transverse lie, prematurity, polyhydramnios, twins, high presenting part, ARM.
Transfer
Exaggerated Sims (not knee–chest) for ambulance transfer. Main harm = cord compression + vasospasm → fetal hypoxia.
What & Why

Shoulder dystocia = an obstetric emergency where, after the head delivers, the anterior shoulder becomes impacted behind the maternal pubic symphysis and gentle axial traction fails to release it. The clock starts the moment the head is out — with the cord compressed + chest unable to expand, the baby faces rapid hypoxia (~47% of shoulder-dystocia deaths occur within 5 minutes of the head delivering).

Definition: a vaginal cephalic delivery that requires additional obstetric manoeuvres after gentle axial traction fails (head-to-body delivery prolonged, classically >60 seconds). The mechanical problem is a BONY impaction (shoulder vs pubic symphysis), not soft-tissue — so the manoeuvres work by changing pelvic geometry or rotating/reducing the shoulder diameter, and simply pulling harder makes it worse.
Recognition & Risk Factors
🐢 Recognition
  • “Turtle-neck” sign — the head delivers then RETRACTS back against the perineum
  • Failure of restitution + failure of the shoulders to deliver with routine traction
  • → prompt recognition, then a systematic manoeuvre sequence (HELPERR)
Risk factors (but prediction is POOR)
  • Pre-labour: macrosomia, maternal diabetes (most important associated factor), obesity/excess weight gain, previous shoulder dystocia (strong recurrence), post-dates
  • Intrapartum: prolonged first/second stage, instrumental delivery, oxytocin augmentation
  • Most shoulder dystocia is UNPREDICTABLE — every attendant must be ready; prediction alone doesn't justify induction/caesarean
Management — the HELPERR Sequence (RCOG GTG42)
📷 Image placeholder — Shoulder dystocia manoeuvres — McRoberts (hyperflexed hips) + suprapubic pressure → internal rotation (Rubin II/Woods’) → delivery of the posterior arm; NO fundal pressure

L — Legs (McRoberts')McRoberts' — FIRST-LINE: lay flat, remove pillows, hyperflex the hips (knees to chest), an assistant each side. Rotates the symphysis upward → frees the shoulder. ~90% effective, least invasive → always first.
P — suprapubic PressureAn assistant applies suprapubic pressure over the anterior shoulder (downward + lateral, “CPR-style”) to push it under the symphysis. Combined with McRoberts'.

Third-line / last resort (all above fail): cleidotomy (deliberate clavicle fracture), symphysiotomy, or the Zavanelli manoeuvre (replace the head into the uterus → emergency caesarean).
Complications & Exam Pearls
👶 Fetal
  • Brachial plexus injury — Erb's palsy (C5–C6) = “waiter's tip” (common, usually resolves); Klumpke's palsy (C8–T1) = “claw hand” (rarer)
  • Fractures — clavicle + humerus
  • Hypoxia → hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy or death
🤰 Maternal
  • Postpartum haemorrhage + perineal/third–fourth-degree tears (the main maternal risks)
  • Symphyseal separation / femoral neuropathy from McRoberts'
  • Document everything — time of head/body delivery, manoeuvres + order, which shoulder was anterior, cord gases, staff (medicolegal)

Anterior shoulder impacted behind the pubic symphysis after the head delivers — a BONY problem.
Recognition
“Turtle-neck sign” (head retracts).
First-line
McRoberts' (~90% effective) + suprapubic pressure. Know the HELPERR order.
NEVER
Fundal pressure (uterine rupture); excessive downward traction (brachial plexus injury).

Diabetes + macrosomia = classic combo, but most cases unpredictable. Erb's (C5–6) = “waiter's tip”; Klumpke's (C8–T1) = “claw hand”.

Deliver the posterior arm = highly effective; Zavanelli (replace head → caesarean) = last resort. Maternal complications = PPH + perineal tears. Document everything.

Interventions to start or assist delivery and their complications — induction of labour, caesarean section and perineal trauma.

What & Why

Induction of labour (IOL) = artificial initiation of labour before it starts spontaneously — when continuing the pregnancy poses more risk than delivering. Common (~1 in 3 UK births). The whole approach is governed by one question — is the cervix ready? (the Bishop score), which dictates the method.

The core principle: you can't force labour on a closed, unfavourable cervix without ripening it first → IOL is a two-part process: ripen the cervix, then stimulate contractions. The Bishop score tells you where a woman sits on that path.
The Decisive Fork — the Bishop Score (NICE NG207)

The Bishop score assesses cervical readiness on vaginal exam + decides which method is offered first. Components: cervical dilatation, effacement/length, consistency, position, and station of the presenting part.

Bishop scoreInterpretationImplication
≤6Unfavourable (“unripe”) cervixNeeds cervical ripening first (prostaglandin or mechanical)
>6 (≥8 = favourable)Favourable (“ripe”) cervixReady for amniotomy + oxytocin
Exam framing: low Bishop score → ripen with dinoprostone first; high/favourable → straight to ARM + oxytocin. This single fork organises the entire management.
Indications & Methods
📋 Indications
  • Prolonged pregnancy — commonest; offer IOL at 41–42 weeks (reduce stillbirth)
  • Prelabour rupture of membranes at term (PROM — reduce infection)
  • Maternal: pre-eclampsia/hypertension, diabetes, obstetric cholestasis
  • Fetal growth restriction / concerning surveillance; intrauterine fetal death; twin/complicated pregnancy
  • Membrane sweep = adjunct (not formal IOL), from ~39–41 weeks
🛠️ Methods
  • Ripening (Bishop ≤6): vaginal DINOPROSTONE (PGE2) — tablet/gel/controlled-release pessary (standard 1st-line); or low-dose oral misoprostol (25 microgram)
  • Mechanical (balloon catheter/osmotic dilator) — if pharmacological unsuitable (hyperstimulation risk, previous caesarean); less hyperstimulation than prostaglandins
  • Favourable cervix (>6): amniotomy (ARM) + IV oxytocin (Syntocinon), titrated to ~4 contractions/10 min
  • ARM ± oxytocin is NOT the primary method on an unfavourable cervix
Monitoring & Complications
📷 Image placeholder — CTG in uterine hyperstimulation — >5 contractions/10 min with late decelerations/reduced variability; read systematically (DR C BRAVADO) → stop oxytocin/remove pessary and give tocolysis
Monitoring: Bishop score before + during; continuous CTG during active induction (prostaglandin/oxytocin) — detects fetal distress + hyperstimulation; watch contraction frequency on oxytocin.
Uterine hyperstimulation — the key IOL complication: excessive contraction frequency/duration → reduced placental perfusion → fetal distress (rarely uterine rupture). Management: stop/remove the inducing agent (remove pessary, stop oxytocin) + consider tocolysis (terbutaline); continuous CTG; escalate.
Other complications: failed induction (→ re-attempt ripening or caesarean); cord prolapse at amniotomy (esp. high presenting part); more instrumental/caesarean delivery; PPH (atony after prolonged oxytocin); infection (prolonged ROM); often more painful than spontaneous labour.
Contraindications & Exam Pearls
Contraindications (avoid vaginal delivery / caution): placenta praevia, vasa praevia, cord presentation; transverse/abnormal lie, malpresentation; previous classical (vertical) caesarean or significant uterine surgery; active primary genital herpes. Prostaglandins used cautiously with a previous caesarean scar (uterine-rupture risk → mechanical often preferred).
The fork
Bishop ≤6 → ripen (dinoprostone/misoprostol or mechanical); >6 → ARM + oxytocin.
Ripening agent
Vaginal dinoprostone (PGE2) is standard; mechanical (balloon) causes LESS hyperstimulation → favoured with previous caesarean/hyperstimulation risk.

Membrane sweep = adjunct ~39–41 weeks; post-dates → offer IOL at 41–42 weeks.
Hyperstimulation
The key complication → remove agent/stop oxytocin + tocolysis (terbutaline) + CTG.
Cautions
ARM ± oxytocin not first-line on an unfavourable cervix; amniotomy risks cord prolapse (high presenting part); failed induction → caesarean; oxytocin target = 4 contractions/10 min.
What & Why

Caesarean section = delivery through incisions in the abdominal wall + uterus rather than vaginally — one of the commonest major operations on women. Two frameworks dominate: the urgency categories (1–4) (how fast to deliver) + the anatomical layers crossed. Around it sits VBAC (can she deliver vaginally next time?).

The Decisive Fork — How Urgent Is It? (NICE NG192)

Category 1 triggers: suspected uterine rupture, major placental abruption, cord prolapse, fetal hypoxia, persistent fetal bradycardia.
Nuance: Category 2 = “within 75 minutes,” but for confirmed/suspected acute fetal compromise (spanning Cat 1 + some Cat 2), deliver within 30 minutes where possible. 75 min is the Cat 2 audit standard; a compromised fetus in Cat 2 is still pushed toward 30.
Types & Anatomical Layers
📷 Image placeholder — Caesarean layers at LSCS — skin → anterior rectus sheath → rectus abdominis (split at the linea alba and retracted, NOT cut) → transversalis fascia → peritoneum → bladder reflected → lower-segment uterine incision
🔪 Types
  • Lower segment (LSCS) — ~99%: transverse incision in the lower segment; lower future-rupture risk, less bleeding, better healing
  • Classical: longitudinal (vertical) upper-segment incision — for very preterm, some transverse lie, anterior praevia/accreta, obstructing fibroids; higher future rupture risk → contraindicates VBAC
🩻 Layers crossed (anatomy trap)
  • Skin/fascia → anterior rectus sheath (incised)
  • Rectus abdominis — NOT cut: separated + pushed laterally after opening the linea alba
  • Transversalis fascia → extraperitoneal connective tissue → peritoneum → uterus
  • (Bladder reflected inferiorly off the lower segment before the uterine incision)
Indications & VBAC
📋 Indications
  • Maternal: previous caesarean (esp. classical), request, obstructing fibroids, active primary herpes, cardiac/medical disease
  • Fetal: breech, transverse/abnormal lie, fetal compromise, twin with non-cephalic twin 1
  • Placental: placenta praevia (major/grade 3–4), accreta, vasa praevia
  • Labour: failure to progress, cord prolapse, previous severe shoulder dystocia; HIV with viral load >50
🔄 VBAC
  • Planned VBAC appropriate at ≥37 weeks with a single previous lower-segment caesarean
  • Contraindicated: previous uterine rupture or previous classical (vertical) scar
  • Main serious risk = uterine rupture (higher than elective repeat CS, but absolute risk low ~0.5%); success ~72–75%
  • Induction/augmentation raises rupture risk → prostaglandins used cautiously
Complications & Exam Pearls
Complications: intra-operative — haemorrhage, bladder/bowel/ureteric injury, incision extension; post-operative — infection (wound, endometritis, UTI), VTE (thromboprophylaxis needed), ileus; future pregnancy — uterine rupture, placenta praevia/accreta (scar implantation), repeat caesarean, adhesions; neonatal — transient tachypnoea of the newborn, iatrogenic prematurity if dates wrong.
Categories
Cat 1 = 30 min; Cat 2 = 75 min; Cat 3 = stable/expedited; Cat 4 = elective. Cat 1 triggers: uterine rupture, major abruption, cord prolapse, fetal hypoxia/bradycardia.
Types
LSCS = 99% (lower rupture risk); classical = vertical upper-segment, higher rupture risk → contraindicates VBAC.
Anatomy
Rectus abdominis is NOT cut — split at the linea alba + retracted laterally.
VBAC
OK with one previous lower-segment CS at ≥37 weeks; contraindicated by previous rupture or classical scar; uterine rupture is the feared complication.
Scar risks
Placenta praevia/accreta risk rises with each caesarean (scar implantation); VTE prophylaxis essential post-caesarean.
What & Why

Perineal tear = a laceration between the vagina + anus during vaginal delivery. The classification is a fixed ladder (1st → 4th degree); the higher grades — involving the anal sphincter (OASIS) — carry a risk of long-term faecal incontinence.

The organising principle: the grade is defined by which structure the tear reaches — skin → muscle → anal sphincter → rectal mucosa — and the grade dictates where + by whom it's repaired.

Risk Factors & Management
Risk factors
  • Primigravida / first vaginal birth (strongest — OASIS ~6% primip vs ~1.7% multip)
  • Large baby (macrosomia); precipitate labour; shoulder dystocia
  • Instrumental delivery — esp. FORCEPS (> ventouse for OASIS)
  • Prolonged second stage, occipito-posterior position
💊 Management
  • 1st: no suturing; 2nd: sutured on the ward
  • 3rd/4th (OASIS): repair in THEATRE under regional/general anaesthesia by a trained clinician
  • EAS: end-to-end or overlap (equivalent); IAS repaired separately end-to-end
  • Post-OASIS: broad-spectrum antibiotics; laxatives (reduce dehiscence; NO routine bulking agent); physiotherapy; digital rectal exam after repair; perineal-clinic follow-up (discuss future delivery mode)

Complications: short-term — bleeding, infection, wound dehiscence, pain, urinary retention; long-term (the ones that matter) — faecal urgency/incontinence, flatus incontinence, dyspareunia, perineal pain, rectovaginal fistula (4th degree), psychological impact.

Deepest structure: 1st skin → 2nd muscle → 3rd anal sphincter → 4th rectal mucosa. OASIS = 3rd + 4th.

Mediolateral episiotomy (60°) for prevention, esp. instrumental; forceps > ventouse for OASIS; primigravida is the key risk factor; feared long-term complication = faecal incontinence.

Overview — postpartum complications
Complications arising after delivery — the puerperium — spanning haemorrhage, infection, endocrine and psychiatric disease.
The organising principle: the postnatal woman can deteriorate rapidly. Work through the common causes by system: bleeding (PPH), fever/sepsis (puerperal pyrexia), mood/psychosis, and endocrine (thyroiditis).

What & Why

Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) = excessive bleeding from the genital tract after delivery — the leading cause of maternal death worldwide and a core obstetric emergency. It’s common, often unpredictable (most cases occur in women with NO risk factors), and the response is a time-critical, protocolised escalation — mechanical → medical → surgical. The framework for the cause is the 4 T’s, and the single most important is Tone.

The core principle: after the placenta delivers, the uterus must contract to clamp the spiral arteries at the placental bed (“physiological ligature”). If it doesn’t — uterine atony — those vessels bleed freely. This is why a ‘boggy’ uterus that won’t contract is the commonest cause, and why the first interventions all aim to make the uterus contract.
Definitions (RCOG Green-top 52)
  • PPH = blood loss ≥500 mL from the genital tract after delivery
  • Primary PPH — within 24 hours of birth
  • Secondary PPH — from 24 hours to 6–12 weeks postpartum; typically retained placental tissue or endometritis (infection — not “endometriosis”)
  • Severity: Minor = 500–1000 mL (no shock); Major = >1000 mL or any volume with shock → moderate 1000–2000 mL / severe >2000 mL
Lochia vs PPH: lochia is the normal postpartum discharge that reduces over ~6 weeks. Bleeding <500 mL with no shock is likely lochia. Ultrasound if lochia persists beyond 6 weeks (?retained products).

What & Why

Puerperal pyrexia = fever in the postpartum period — traditionally a temperature ≥38°C in the first 14 days after delivery (some definitions span the puerperium to 6 weeks). It matters because postpartum sepsis remains a leading cause of maternal death — the classic “childbed fever” — and a systematic “where is the source?” approach is needed. The single most important cause is endometritis.

The core concern: the postpartum uterus has a raw placental bed and an open cervix — a ready portal for ascending infection. Genital tract sepsis can escalate rapidly (especially Group A Streptococcus) → a febrile new mother is treated with urgency, not reassurance.

Postpartum Endometritis — The Key Cause
  • Uterine infection, usually from bacteria ascending from the lower genital/GI tract — typically polymicrobial (mixed aerobes + anaerobes)
  • Risk factors: caesarean section (the biggest), prolonged rupture of membranes, prolonged labour, retained products, multiple vaginal examinations, group B Streptococcus carriage, obesity, diabetes
  • Features: fever, lower abdominal/uterine tenderness, offensive/heavy lochia, secondary PPH, malaise
Investigations
  • Observations / sepsis screen — temp, HR, RR, BP (a MEOWS chart flags deterioration)
  • Bloods — FBC, CRP, U&E, lactate, blood cultures
  • High vaginal + endocervical swabs (and placental swab if available)
  • MSU (UTI); wound swab if wound infection; breast exam (mastitis)
  • Consider ultrasound (retained products, pelvic collection) and CTPA/Doppler if VTE suspected; throat swab if Group A Strep suspected
Management
Assess severity — use the sepsis pathway. If severe sepsis (hypotension, tachycardia, raised lactate, breathlessness) → initiate the Sepsis Six and escalate urgently (RCOG GTG64).
💊 Endometritis / genital tract sepsis

  • Clindamycin + gentamicin IV — first-line, continued until afebrile for >24 h (oral continuation usually not needed)
  • Severe sepsis → broader cover (IV piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem ± clindamycin for its antitoxin effect in Group A Strep) — follow local microbiology
🎯 Treat the specific source
  • Antibiotics for UTI / wound / mastitis
  • Anticoagulation for VTE
  • ERPC if retained tissue is driving endometritis
  • Supportive: fluids, antipyretics, monitoring
Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) — highly virulent; low threshold for aggressive treatment + infection-control precautions.

What & Why

Puerperal (postpartum) psychosis = a severe, acute psychiatric emergency in the early postpartum period, characterised by psychosis, mania and mood disturbance. It is the most serious psychiatric disorder of childbirth — carrying real risk of suicide and infanticide/harm to the baby — and demands immediate psychiatric admission, ideally to a specialist Mother & Baby Unit.

The key framing: puerperal psychosis is strongly linked to bipolar affective disorder — often the first presentation of, or a relapse of, bipolar illness triggered by childbirth. A personal/family history of bipolar disorder or previous puerperal psychosis is the biggest risk factor.

Presentation
  • Onset within ~2–3 weeks of birth (often abrupt, within the first few days)
  • Severe mood swings — mania and/or depression

Prognosis: generally good with prompt treatment (most recover fully), but high recurrence in future pregnancies + risk of subsequent bipolar episodes → pre-conception counselling + a perinatal mental health plan matter.

What & Why

Postpartum thyroiditis (PPT) = a transient autoimmune inflammation of the thyroid within 12 months of delivery in a previously euthyroid woman (no Graves’ or toxic nodule). It’s common (~5–10%), easily missed (symptoms dismissed as new-baby stress), and a classic exam pattern: a destructive thyroiditis producing a hyperthyroid phase then a hypothyroid phase, each managed differently.

The core mechanism: autoimmune lymphocytic destruction of thyroid follicles → preformed hormone leaks out → a transient thyrotoxic phase (this is release, not overproduction — why antithyroid drugs don’t work). Once stores deplete → a hypothyroid phase → then usually recovery. TPO antibodies drive it (~90%).

  • TPO antibodies present in ~90% — and TPO-positivity in pregnancy predicts who develops PPT (~50% of TPO-positive women do)

Overview — gynaecological cancers
The four gynaecological malignancies — endometrial, ovarian, cervical and vulval — differ in risk factors, presentation and screening/prevention.
The organising principle: link each cancer to its hallmark. Endometrial → postmenopausal bleeding (unopposed oestrogen); ovarian → vague late symptoms + ↑CA-125; cervical → HPV, screened & vaccine-preventable; vulval → VIN/lichen sclerosus, elderly.

What & Why

Endometrial cancer = a malignancy of the uterine lining — the commonest gynaecological cancer in the UK + the 4th commonest cancer in women. Overwhelmingly a disease of postmenopausal women (peak 60s–70s).

The single highest-yield reflex: postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. It announces itself early + loudly through abnormal bleeding → usually presents at a curable stage.
The through-line for the common type: UNOPPOSED OESTROGEN. Oestrogen drives endometrial proliferation; progesterone opposes it. Anything raising the oestrogen-to-progesterone ratio raises risk.

⬆️ Increase risk

  • PCOS (chronic anovulation → unopposed oestrogen)
  • Oestrogen-only HRT (no progestogen, with a uterus)

  • Premenopausal: intermenstrual bleeding, or heavier/irregular menstrual bleeding
  • Abnormal discharge or pyometra (postmenopausal)
  • Late disease: pelvic pain, weight loss

What & Why

Ovarian cancer = a malignancy of the ovary (often the fallopian tube fimbriae for the commonest subtype). The leading cause of gynaecological-cancer death in the UK — the “silent killer”.

Presents LATE, poor prognosis — the exact mirror of endometrial cancer. Vague symptoms mistaken for IBS or ageing → ~⅔ diagnosed at advanced stage.
The unifying theme: the “incessant ovulation” hypothesis. Each ovulation ruptures + repairs the ovarian surface; cumulative lifetime ovulations drive malignant transformation. Anything reducing lifetime ovulations is protective.

What & Why

Cervical cancer = a malignancy of the cervix — the cancer where you must know two parallel stories: the disease itself + the NHS screening/vaccination programme built to prevent it. Affects young women (peak 30s–40s).

The central fact: persistent high-risk HPV causes nearly all cervical cancer. Types 16 + 18 cause ~70%. It is preventable (vaccine + screening) → the exam heavily weights prevention over treatment.

  • Loss of both brakes → uncontrolled cervical epithelial proliferation → CIN → invasive cancer
🔬 Histology fork
  • Squamous cell carcinoma (~70–80%) — arises at the transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction); best detected by screening
  • Adenocarcinoma (~20%) — glandular, arises higher in the canal → harder to catch on screening

  • BIOPSY is essential — every suspicious vulval lesion, and any suspicious area within lichen sclerosus

  • Staging: exam ± EUA, MRI/CT; FIGO staged; spreads via the inguinal (groin) nodes — nodal status is the dominant prognostic factor

🔪 VIN (pre-invasive)
  • uVIN / vulval HSIL: local surgical excision, or topical imiquimod in selected counselled women (after excluding occult invasion); laser in some cases
  • dVIN: excision — treated more aggressively (high, fast progression risk); optimise lichen sclerosus treatment
🏥 Invasive vulval cancer
  • Surgery is the cornerstone — wide local excision (or radical vulvectomy for larger/multifocal) aiming for clear margins, extended to include adjacent dVIN/lichen sclerosus
  • Groin nodes: sentinel lymph node biopsy for early unifocal tumours; inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy if involved/high-risk
  • Radiotherapy ± chemotherapy — adjuvant for node-positive/high-risk, or primary chemoradiation for advanced/unresectable

Two roads
HPV/uVIN (younger) vs lichen sclerosus/dVIN (older, p53-mutated) — this fork is the entire topic.
dVIN
Rarer but far more dangerous — fast progression, easily mistaken for benign dermatosis. Don't be reassured by “just lichen sclerosus”.
Histology
~90% squamous cell carcinoma; HPV 16 is the key oncogenic type (as in cervix).

Itchy white atrophic “cigarette-paper” plaques, figure-of-eight, potent topical steroid, ~5% → cancer — biopsy any non-healing area.
Next step
Biopsy every suspicious vulval lesion — the exam-safe answer.
Spread
To inguinal nodes; nodal status drives prognosis; sentinel node biopsy in early disease.
Stem
Elderly woman, long-standing vulval itch, now a lump/ulcer → vulval cancer until proven otherwise.
The trio
Cervical = young/HPV; endometrial = obese/PMB; vulval = elderly/itch; ovarian = late/silent.

What & Why

Endometriosis = ENDOMETRIAL-like tissue OUTSIDE the uterine cavity (pelvis + beyond) — an oestrogen-dependent, chronic inflammatory condition causing pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, and subfertility. A cyst in the ovary = an endometrioma (“chocolate cyst”); within the myometrium = adenomyosis.

The core concept — ectopic endometrium that still RESPONDS to the cycle: it proliferates, breaks down + bleeds each cycle, but the blood has nowhere to escape → cyclical inflammation, fibrosis, adhesions, scarring. Hence: (1) CYCLICAL pain (tracks menstruation) becoming chronic (adhesions); (2) location-specific symptoms (pouch of Douglas → deep dyspareunia; bowel → dyschezia; bladder → dysuria; ovary → endometrioma); (3) severity correlates POORLY with disease extent; and (4) a major cause of SUBFERTILITY.

Infections of the female genital tract — pelvic inflammatory disease (upper tract) and the common causes of abnormal discharge (BV, trichomonas).

What & Why

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) = infection and inflammation of the upper female genital tract — uterus (endometritis), fallopian tubes (salpingitis), ovaries (oophoritis) and surrounding peritoneum. It is usually caused by a sexually transmitted infection ascending from the endocervix, is frequently under-diagnosed (non-specific symptoms), and its long-term complications — infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain — are serious and preventable.

The core route: infection ascends from the endocervix upwards. This is why STIs are the main cause, and why the classic sign is cervical motion tenderness (moving the inflamed structures hurts).
Examinable essence: a LOW threshold to treat empirically — don’t wait for confirmation, the cost of missing it is high — plus knowing the antibiotic regimens.

What & Why

Bacterial vaginosis (BV) = an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria in the vagina caused by loss of the protective lactobacilli. It is the commonest cause of abnormal vaginal discharge in women of reproductive age. Although often trivial, it raises the risk of acquiring STIs and causes pregnancy complications (preterm birth, miscarriage). Crucially, BV is NOT a sexually transmitted infection — it’s a disturbance of the vaginal flora.

The core mechanism: healthy lactobacilli produce lactic acid → keep pH acidic (<4.5), suppressing other bacteria. When lactobacilli are lost, the pH rises (alkaline), favouring overgrowth of anaerobes — chiefly Gardnerella vaginalis. Everything about BV flows from this loss of acidity → anaerobic overgrowth.

  • Excessive vaginal cleaning / douching (washes out lactobacilli)
  • Recent antibiotics
  • Smoking
  • Copper intrauterine device (IUD)
Clinical Features
  • ~50% are asymptomatic
  • Thin, white, homogenous discharge coating the vaginal walls
  • Fishy odour — often worse after sex/menstruation (alkaline semen/blood raises pH)
  • No significant itching or soreness (distinguishes from candida)
  • Positive “whiff test” — adding potassium hydroxide (KOH) releases a fishy amine odour

Diagnose BV if ≥3 of the 4 Amsel’s criteria are present:
  • Thin, white, homogenous discharge
  • Vaginal pH >4.5
  • Clue cells on microscopy — vaginal epithelial cells stippled with adherent bacteria (a “granular/moth-eaten” cell border)
  • Positive whiff test (fishy odour with KOH)
The Nugent score / Hay-Ison Gram-stain grading is the laboratory alternative.

  • Increased risk of acquiring STIs (including HIV) — the raised pH + loss of protection
  • In pregnancy: miscarriage, preterm birth, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PROM), chorioamnionitis, low birth weight, postpartum endometritis
  • Post-procedural infection (e.g. after termination/surgery)
Note: the pregnancy complication is postpartum endometritis (uterine infection) — not “endometriosis”.

  • Asymptomatic BV usually needs no treatment (except before some gynae procedures, or in pregnancy with risk factors)
  • First-line: oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5–7 days
  • Alternatives: metronidazole 2 g single oral dose (aids adherence; slightly less effective); topical metronidazole gel or topical clindamycin cream

  • Newer evidence questions whether it’s truly disulfiram-like, but the exam-safe answer remains “avoid alcohol”
🧼 Advice + partners
  • Avoid vaginal douching / soaps / shower gels inside the vagina (disrupt flora) — key prevention
  • Do NOT routinely treat partners — treating male partners doesn’t reduce recurrence
Pregnancy: treat symptomatic BV (given adverse outcomes) — oral metronidazole (avoid the high-dose 2 g single regimen) or topical; metronidazole is considered low-risk in pregnancy.
Recurrence is common (~50–70% within a year) — consider avoiding triggers and, in some, suppressive regimens.

What & Why

Trichomoniasis = a sexually transmitted infection caused by Trichomonas vaginalis — a flagellated protozoan parasite (not a bacterium). It’s a common STI, the classic cause of a frothy yellow-green discharge with a “strawberry cervix”, and it increases HIV transmission risk and causes adverse pregnancy outcomes (preterm birth, low birth weight). Being a true STI, it requires partner treatment and contact tracing — a key distinction from BV.

The key contrast: trichomonas and BV both raise pH >4.5 and can both smell fishy — but trichomonas is a sexually transmitted parasite (treat partners, contact-trace), whereas BV is a flora disturbance (don’t treat partners). Candida has a normal pH (<4.5).

Overview — benign vulvovaginal & cervical conditions
Common benign conditions of the vulva, vagina and cervix — usually clinical diagnoses that are important to recognise, reassure or treat.
The organising principle: benign, but must be distinguished from sinister mimics (postmenopausal bleeding, cervical cancer).

What & Why

Atrophic vaginitis = thinning, drying + inflammation of the vaginal/vulval/urethral tissues due to OESTROGEN DEFICIENCY — most commonly after the MENOPAUSE. The modern term is GENITOURINARY SYNDROME OF MENOPAUSE (GSM), capturing that it affects the vulva, vagina, urethra + bladder (not just the vagina).

The core concept — these tissues are OESTROGEN-DEPENDENT: oestrogen maintains a thick, elastic, well-lubricated, glycogen-rich epithelium with an acidic pH (lactobacilli → lactic acid). When oestrogen falls, the tissues thin, lose elasticity, dry out, and the pH RISES (alkaline) → vaginal dryness, itch, soreness, DYSPAREUNIA, plus urinary symptoms (urgency, frequency, dysuria, recurrent UTIs).
Two key points: (1) it's CHRONIC + PROGRESSIVE + does NOT self-resolve (unlike flushes) → needs ongoing treatment; and (2) it's massively UNDER-reported → ask about it. Mainstay = TOPICAL vaginal OESTROGEN (safe, minimal systemic absorption). Affects >50% of post-menopausal women. Reflex: a post-menopausal woman with vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, or recurrent UTIs = atrophic vaginitis/GSM → moisturisers + topical oestrogen.

Causes of oestrogen deficiency: MENOPAUSE (commonest); also premature ovarian insufficiency, post-oophorectomy, breastfeeding (lactation), anti-oestrogen drugs (GnRH agonists, aromatase inhibitors, tamoxifen), post-chemo/radiotherapy.
Why the name changed: GSM replaced “atrophic vaginitis” because it also causes URINARY symptoms + recurrent UTIs (the urethra/bladder trigone are oestrogen-sensitive too).
The rule: vaginal dryness/itch/soreness + DYSPAREUNIA + urinary symptoms (recurrent UTIs) in a low-oestrogen state (usually post-menopausal) = atrophic vaginitis/GSM.
Examination, Investigations & the Key Differential

Examination: a PALE, THIN, DRY vaginal epithelium; loss of rugae (smooth); reduced elasticity; narrowed/shortened vagina; petechiae/friability/contact bleeding; pale/atrophic vulva. A CLINICAL diagnosis — usually no tests. Vaginal pH raised/alkaline; exclude infection (candida, bacterial vaginosis, STIs) if discharge; urine culture if UTI symptoms.
The CRUCIAL differential — POST-MENOPAUSAL BLEEDING: atrophy is a common cause, BUT post-menopausal bleeding must be investigated to EXCLUDE ENDOMETRIAL CANCER first → 2-week-wait referral + transvaginal ultrasound (endometrial thickness) ± biopsy → only attribute bleeding to atrophy once cancer is excluded.
Management (NICE NG23 — Guideline-Verified)
The principle: non-hormonal (moisturisers/lubricants) + TOPICAL VAGINAL OESTROGEN (the mainstay — safe, minimal systemic absorption, can be long-term); it's chronic → symptoms recur if treatment stops.
🧴 Non-hormonal (first-line/adjunct)
  • Vaginal MOISTURISERS (regular — e.g. hyaluronic-acid) + LUBRICANTS (for intercourse)
  • First-line for mild symptoms, or when oestrogen is contraindicated/declined
💊 Topical vaginal oestrogen (mainstay)
  • Low-dose vaginal oestrogen (cream, pessary, or ring) → directly restores the epithelium
  • Minimal systemic absorption → long-term use, NO progestogen needed, no systemic HRT risks
  • Takes ~3 months for full benefit; recurs when stopped
Systemic HRT: if also having systemic menopausal symptoms (flushes), systemic HRT helps GSM too — but vaginal oestrogen can be ADDED if genitourinary symptoms persist. Alternatives: vaginal DHEA (prasterone); ospemifene (an oral SERM). Breast cancer (esp. on aromatase inhibitors): non-hormonal first; vaginal oestrogen only after oncology discussion.
The rule: moisturisers + lubricants + TOPICAL VAGINAL OESTROGEN (mainstay — safe, no progestogen needed, long-term); add to systemic HRT if needed; DHEA/ospemifene as alternatives; recurs if stopped.

What & Why

Bartholin's and Nabothian cysts are both common, BENIGN mucus-retention cysts — but at different sites: Bartholin's = at the VULVA (vaginal opening), Nabothian = on the CERVIX. Both arise from blockage of a mucus-secreting gland/duct → trapped mucus → a cyst.

Both usually harmless + incidental — the clinical importance is recognising them as benign (+ managing a Bartholin's ABSCESS if it becomes infected). Reflex: a unilateral cyst/swelling at the vaginal opening = Bartholin's; a smooth whitish bump on the cervix = Nabothian.
Bartholin's Cyst & Abscess

The Bartholin's (greater vestibular) glands sit bilaterally at the vaginal introitus (~4 and 8 o'clock) + secrete mucus for lubrication → duct blocks → mucus retention → a cyst; if infected → an abscess.

🔎 Cyst vs abscess
  • Cyst: UNILATERAL, fluid-filled, 1–4 cm, near the vaginal opening; often soft, painless/mildly uncomfortable
  • Abscess (infected): HOT, TENDER, RED, painful, rapidly enlarging
  • E. coli = commonest cause (usually polymicrobial; consider STI testing — gonorrhoea/chlamydia)
💊 Management
  • CLINICAL diagnosis
  • Cyst: conservative — hygiene, analgesia, WARM COMPRESSES (many resolve)
  • Abscess: ANTIBIOTICS + SWAB (culture) + surgical drainage — WORD CATHETER (balloon catheter → epithelialised tract) or MARSUPIALISATION (suture the cyst edges open — for recurrence)
The malignancy caveat: a Bartholin's mass in a woman OVER ~40 → consider biopsy/excision to exclude a (rare) Bartholin's gland CARCINOMA.
The rule: unilateral fluid-filled cyst (1–4 cm) at the vaginal opening = Bartholin's; hot/tender/red = abscess (E. coli commonest) → antibiotics + swab + word catheter/marsupialisation; biopsy if >40.
Nabothian Cyst

A Nabothian cyst forms on the cervix when the squamous epithelium of the ectocervix grows over the mucus-producing columnar epithelium of the endocervix (squamous metaplasia at the transformation zone) → trapping mucus underneath → a cyst. Triggers: after childbirth, minor trauma, or cervicitis.

🔎 Features
  • Often found INCIDENTALLY on speculum exam
  • Typically ASYMPTOMATIC; rarely become large
  • SMOOTH, ROUNDED, WHITISH/YELLOW bumps on the cervix near the os
🛋️ Management
  • benign — no treatment needed (they persist harmlessly; reassure)
  • COLPOSCOPY if the diagnosis is unsure
  • May be EXCISED/BIOPSIED only if doubt / to exclude other pathology
The rule: smooth, whitish/yellow bumps on the cervix near the os, incidental + asymptomatic = Nabothian cysts → reassure (benign, no treatment); colposcopy/biopsy only if uncertain.

What & Why

Cervical ectropion (cervical ectopy / “erosion”) = a benign condition where the COLUMNAR epithelium of the endocervix extends OUT onto the ectocervix — the delicate glandular lining exposed on the outer cervix. It is NOT a true erosion/ulcer (the old name is misleading) — just endocervical lining in an outer location.

The core concept — which epithelium is where: the ectocervix (outer) is tough stratified SQUAMOUS; the endocervix (canal) is delicate, mucus-secreting COLUMNAR. Under HIGH-OESTROGEN states (puberty, the combined pill, pregnancy) the squamocolumnar junction moves OUTWARD → fragile columnar epithelium is exposed on the ectocervix. Because it's thin, vascular + mucus-producing, it bleeds easily on contact + produces more discharge → POST-COITAL bleeding + increased discharge.
Two key points: (1) it's a normal, benign, OESTROGEN-driven finding (young women on the pill + in pregnancy), and (2) the crucial task is to EXCLUDE serious causes — cervical cancer + infection (STIs) — before attributing symptoms to ectropion. Reflex: post-coital bleeding + discharge in a young pill-user, with a red ring around the os = ectropion → but exclude cancer/STI first.

Clinical Features & Excluding the Sinister Causes

🚨 Must EXCLUDE first
  • CERVICAL CANCER — speculum, up-to-date SMEAR, colposcopy if suspicious
  • Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) — smear/colposcopy
  • Infection/STIs — swabs (chlamydia, gonorrhoea)

Management
The principle: benign → REASSURE + no treatment if asymptomatic; if symptomatic → remove/reduce oestrogen (stop/change the pill) or ABLATE the ectropion; always exclude sinister causes first.

  • ABLATION — cryotherapy / cautery / silver nitrate / diathermy to the columnar epithelium (definitive for persistent symptoms)
  • In pregnancy: usually conservative (regresses after delivery)
The rule: asymptomatic → reassure; symptomatic → exclude cancer/STI → stop/change the pill or ABLATE (cryotherapy/cautery/silver nitrate); conservative in pregnancy.

OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Menopause & Fe:
Overview — menopause & fertility
The end of reproductive life (menopause / premature ovarian insufficiency) and difficulties achieving pregnancy (subfertility), plus a key complication of assisted reproduction (OHSS).
The organising principle: menopause is a clinical/biochemical diagnosis (↑FSH + symptoms); subfertility needs structured investigation of ovulation, tubes and sperm; OHSS is an iatrogenic emergency after ovulation induction.

What & Why

Menopause = permanent cessation of menstruation from loss of ovarian follicular function — retrospectively defined as 12 months after the last period (average UK age ~51). Premature Ovarian Insufficiency (POI) = the same thing before age 40 — where the calculus flips (HRT becomes a replacement, not an optional symptom treatment).

The core mechanism: ovarian follicles deplete → oestrogen falls → loss of negative feedback → FSH + LH rise. Every symptom flows from oestrogen deficiency; the high FSH is the biochemical fingerprint.

Clinical Features & Diagnosis
🔥 Features (oestrogen deficiency)
  • Vasomotor: hot flushes, night sweats (the hallmark)
  • Menstrual: irregular → absent periods
  • GSM: vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary frequency/urgency, recurrent UTIs
  • Psychological: mood/anxiety/low mood, “brain fog”, poor sleep; reduced libido
  • Long-term: osteoporosis (fractures) + increased cardiovascular disease risk
🔬 Diagnosis (NICE NG23)
  • ≥45 with typical symptoms → diagnose CLINICALLY, NO blood tests (FSH fluctuates, doesn't change management)
  • Consider FSH only if 40–45 with symptoms, <40 (POI), or atypical
  • POI: symptoms + elevated FSH (>30) on 2 samples 4–6 weeks apart
  • POI causes: idiopathic (commonest), iatrogenic (chemo/radio/oophorectomy), autoimmune, genetic (Turner, Fragile X)
Management
📷 Image placeholder — HRT decision tree — uterus present → combined (oestrogen + progestogen); no uterus → oestrogen-only; choose the transdermal route if VTE risk or BMI >30
🌿 Non-hormonal
  • Lifestyle (exercise, weight, reduce alcohol/caffeine/smoking)
  • CBT — now recommended for vasomotor symptoms + low mood (2024 NICE update)
  • SSRIs/SNRIs for flushes (cautiously)
  • Vaginal (topical) oestrogen / moisturisers-lubricants for GSM (safe, long-term)
💊 HRT — the golden rule
  • Uterus present → combined HRT (oestrogen + progestogen) — progestogen protects the endometrium (unopposed oestrogen → hyperplasia/cancer)
  • No uterus → oestrogen-only HRT
  • Transdermal preferred if VTE risk / BMI >30 — transdermal oestrogen doesn't raise VTE risk (no first-pass); oral does
  • Benefits: symptom relief + bone protection
HRT risks (keep in proportion): breast cancer — small increase with COMBINED HRT, duration-related, falls after stopping (oestrogen-only little/none); VTE + stroke raised with ORAL (not transdermal). Do NOT offer HRT for prevention of cardiovascular disease or dementia (2024 NICE) — it's for symptoms/bone.
POI-specific (NICE NG23): offer sex-steroid replacement — HRT or the COCP — until at least ~51 (replaces oestrogen a young woman should have → protects bone + cardiovascular health; the older-woman “HRT risk” narrative doesn't apply). Still need contraception (may occasionally ovulate; HRT isn't contraceptive, the COCP is). Address fertility (donor eggs), bone health (DEXA), psychological support.

What & Why

Subfertility = failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse — affecting ~1 in 7 couples. Investigate both partners, organised around one question: is the problem sperm, egg (ovulation), or the plumbing (tubes)?

Most couples are subfertile (reduced, not zero) — >80% conceive within a year, and about half the rest in the second year → the workup is as much reassurance + timing as pathology.

History, Examination & Investigations (NICE CG156)
📋 History + preconception
  • Both partners together; duration, coital frequency/timing, previous pregnancies
  • Woman: cycle history (regular = likely ovulating), PID/STI, surgery, BMI, meds; Man: previous children, mumps, surgery/trauma, heat
  • Preconception: folic acid, stop smoking/alcohol, optimise BMI (~19–30; lose weight if ≥30), intercourse every 2–3 days
🔬 Investigations
  • Semen analysis (repeat at ~3 months if abnormal — spermatogenesis ~74 days); WHO: volume ≥1.5 mL, conc ≥15 million/mL, motility ≥40%, normal forms ≥4%
  • Mid-luteal progesterone — 7 days before the expected period (day 21 of a 28-day cycle; adjust for length); raised = ovulation
  • If irregular: FSH/LH (day 2–5), prolactin, TSH, testosterone (PCOS), ± AMH (reserve)
  • Tubal patency: HSG (1st-line), HyCoSy, or laparoscopy + dye (if pelvic pathology). Chlamydia screen before instrumentation
Referral: investigate after 1 year; refer earlier (before 1 year) if the woman is ≥36, a known cause, or a predisposing history (PID, cancer treatment, amenorrhoea, undescended testes). Age is the dominant prognostic factor.

🎯 By cause

  • Tubal: tubal surgery (mild) or IVF (bypasses tubes — often preferred for significant damage)
  • Male: mild → IUI/IVF; severe → ICSI; surgical sperm retrieval; donor sperm
🧫 Assisted reproduction
  • IUI — prepared sperm into the uterus (mild male factor, same-sex, donor)
  • IVF — stimulation → egg retrieval → in-vitro fertilisation → embryo transfer
  • ICSI — single sperm injected into the egg (severe male factor)
  • Donor gametes/embryos, surrogacy where appropriate
Unexplained infertility → do NOT offer clomifene/letrozole (no benefit) → continue regular intercourse → offer IVF after 2 years. Key complication of ovulation induction/IVF = OHSS.
Exam Pearls
Definition
No conception after 12 months of regular intercourse; >80% conceive within a year. Investigate BOTH partners; causes ≈ thirds (male/ovulatory/tubal + unexplained).
Core tests
Semen analysis (repeat 3 months if abnormal) + mid-luteal (day 21) progesterone (ovulation) + HSG/laparoscopy (tubes).
Referral
Earlier (before 1 year) if woman ≥36, known cause, or predisposing history.
Ovulation induction
PCOS anovulation → letrozole or clomifene (± metformin).
Traps
Unexplained → NO clomifene/letrozole → IVF after 2 years. Severe male factor → ICSI.
Basics
Optimise BMI, folic acid, stop smoking, intercourse every 2–3 days; chlamydia is the leading tubal cause (screen before instrumentation); OHSS = key complication.
What & Why

OHSS = an iatrogenic, systemic complication of fertility treatment — an exaggerated ovarian response to controlled stimulation. The most serious complication of ovulation induction/IVF (has caused maternal deaths); central danger = massive fluid shift + a prothrombotic state → VTE.

The mechanism (through-line): stimulated ovaries exposed to hCG (the trigger injection, or endogenous hCG of an early pregnancy) release VEGF → increased vascular permeability → fluid leaks into the “third space”. This explains it all: third-space loss (ascites, effusions, oedema); intravascular depletion (hypovolaemia, haemoconcentration, hypotension, AKI); haemoconcentration + prothrombotic → VTE (the feared killer); ovarian enlargement (pain, torsion/rupture risk).
Key trigger: OHSS is hCG-driven → rare without hCG, and it WORSENS if pregnancy occurs (endogenous hCG keeps the ovaries stimulated) — “late” OHSS is pregnancy-associated + more severe.
The Decisive Fork — How Severe? (RCOG GTG5)
GradeFeatures
MildAbdominal bloating/discomfort, mild nausea; ovaries <8 cm
ModerateModerate pain, nausea/vomiting, ultrasound ascites; ovaries 8–12 cm
SevereClinical ascites (± hydrothorax), oliguria, haemoconcentration (haematocrit >45%), hypoproteinaemia; ovaries >12 cm
CriticalTense ascites/large effusions, haematocrit >55%, WCC >25, oligo/anuria, VTE, ARDS, organ failure
Risk factors: PCOS (many follicles), young age, low BMI, high antral follicle count / high AMH, previous OHSS, high follicle number/oestradiol during stimulation, hCG trigger + luteal support, pregnancy.
Presentation & Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — OHSS pathophysiology — hCG → VEGF release → ↑vascular permeability → third-space fluid shift (ascites, haemoconcentration, VTE risk, ovarian enlargement)
🔎 Presentation
  • Abdominal bloating, distension + pain (ovarian enlargement + ascites)
  • Nausea/vomiting, diarrhoea; reduced urine output
  • Shortness of breath (ascites/effusion)
  • Calf swelling / signs of VTE — including unusual sites (upper-limb/neck vein thrombosis)
  • Develops within days of the hCG trigger / egg collection, or later if pregnant
🧪 Investigations
  • FBC — haematocrit (haemoconcentration/severity), WCC
  • U&Es (AKI, electrolytes), LFTs, albumin, coagulation
  • Ultrasound — enlarged ovaries, ascites; CXR if respiratory compromise
  • β-hCG (pregnant? predicts worsening)
  • Exclude mimics: ovarian torsion, ovarian rupture, ectopic pregnancy
Management (RCOG GTG5 — Guideline-Verified)
Principle: usually self-limiting → supportive care while awaiting resolution; priorities = fluid balance, symptom control, and VTE prevention.
🏠 Mild–moderate (outpatient)
  • Analgesia (paracetamol/codeine — avoid NSAIDs if renal compromise); antiemetics
  • Oral fluids to thirst; monitor symptoms, weight, urine output
  • Safety-net + review; VTE risk assessment
🏥 Severe/critical (admit)
  • IV fluids to correct hypovolaemia; monitor fluid balance, U&Es, haematocrit
  • Paracentesis for tense/symptomatic ascites (relieves pain/breathing, improves renal perfusion)
  • VTE prophylaxis — LMWH + stockings — ESSENTIAL (OHSS is strongly prothrombotic; often into pregnancy if she conceives)
  • Human albumin (plasma expander) in some; HDU/ICU for critical; surgery ONLY for torsion/rupture/ectopic (otherwise leave the fragile ovaries alone)
Prevention: identify high-risk (PCOS, high AMH), lower stimulation doses, antagonist protocols with a GnRH-agonist trigger instead of hCG, “freeze-all” embryos (avoid pregnancy hCG that cycle), and cabergoline (reduces VEGF effect).
Exam Pearls
What it is
Iatrogenic complication of ovarian stimulation/IVF: hCG → VEGF → increased vascular permeability → third-space fluid shift.
The picture
Ascites + effusions + hypovolaemia + haemoconcentration + prothrombotic state + enlarged ovaries.
hCG
The trigger — so PREGNANCY worsens it (later, more severe). PCOS / high AMH / young / low BMI = highest risk.
Severity
By haematocrit + ascites: mild bloating → severe (Hct >45%, clinical ascites, oliguria) → critical (Hct >55%, VTE, organ failure).
Management
Supportive + fluid balance + analgesia/antiemetics; severe → IV fluids, paracentesis, and crucially LMWH VTE prophylaxis (essential — OHSS kills via thrombosis, incl. neck/arm veins).
Surgery / prevention
Surgery only for torsion/rupture/ectopic — otherwise leave the ovaries. Prevention: GnRH-agonist trigger, freeze-all, cabergoline.
OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Menstrual Diso:
What & Why

Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) = excessive menstrual loss that interferes with quality of life — defined by impact, not millilitres (the old “≥80 mL” figure is obsolete). A common gynae presentation + frequent cause of iron-deficiency anaemia.

Terminology: “dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB)” is obsolete — HMB is a symptom; you classify the cause with PALM-COEIN.
The Decisive Fork — Structural or Not? (PALM-COEIN)
📷 Image placeholder — PALM-COEIN by exam — bulky irregular non-tender uterus → Leiomyoma; tender boggy symmetrical uterus + dysmenorrhoea → Adenomyosis; heavy bleeding since menarche + easy bruising → Coagulopathy
PALM (structural)COEIN (non-structural)
P — Polyp (endometrial/cervical)C — Coagulopathy (e.g. von Willebrand)
A — AdenomyosisO — Ovulatory dysfunction (PCOS, perimenopause, thyroid)
L — Leiomyoma (fibroids)E — Endometrial (primary endometrial dysfunction)
M — Malignancy & hyperplasiaI — Iatrogenic (copper coil, anticoagulants); N — Not otherwise classified
Exam framing: bulky irregular uterus → fibroids (L); tender boggy symmetrical uterus + dysmenorrhoea → adenomyosis (A); HMB since menarche + easy bruising → coagulopathy (C, von Willebrand); irregular cycles + hirsutism → ovulatory dysfunction (O, PCOS); intermenstrual/postmenopausal bleeding → exclude malignancy (M).
Assessment & Investigations (NICE NG88)
History: nature/impact, related symptoms (pelvic pain/pressure, intermenstrual/postcoital bleeding → structural/malignant), HMB since menarche + bleeding history (→ coagulopathy). Examination: physical (incl. pelvic/speculum) exam before all investigations or an LNG-IUS fitting (exception: low-risk history + non-LNG-IUS treatment can start without exam).
✅ Do
  • FBC for ALL women — in parallel with starting treatment (detect anaemia)
  • Coagulation testing (von Willebrand) only if history suggests (HMB since menarche, bleeding history)
🚫 Don't (routinely)
  • Do NOT routinely test serum ferritin
  • Do NOT do routine female-hormone testing
  • Do NOT test thyroid function unless other thyroid signs
Imaging/hysteroscopy (guided by history): outpatient hysteroscopy if suspected submucosal fibroids/polyps/endometrial pathology (persistent intermenstrual bleeding, cancer risk factors); transvaginal ultrasound for larger structural abnormality; endometrial biopsy if cancer/hyperplasia is a concern (persistent intermenstrual bleeding, ≥45 with treatment failure).
Management (NICE NG88 — Guideline-Verified)
📷 Image placeholder — HMB algorithm — exam + FBC → LNG-IUS first-line → if declined, tranexamic acid/NSAID (no contraception) or COCP/cyclical progestogen (contraception wanted) → ablation/hysterectomy if medical fails and family complete
1st-line: LNG-IUS (Mirena) — if no pathology, fibroids <3 cm not distorting the cavity, or adenomyosis, and long-term use is acceptable. The most effective medical option + the guideline's clear first choice.
💊 If LNG-IUS declined/unsuitable
  • Non-hormonal (contraception NOT wanted): tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic — no cycle effect) or NSAIDs (mefenamic acid — reduce bleeding AND dysmenorrhoea; good if pain co-exists)
  • Hormonal (contraception wanted): combined pill (COCP) or cyclical oral progestogens (norethisterone)
🔧 Surgical/procedural
  • Endometrial ablation — family complete (not if future fertility desired)
  • Hysteroscopic removal of submucosal fibroids/polyps
  • Uterine artery embolisation / myomectomy (fibroids, fertility-sparing)
  • Hysterectomy — definitive but invasive, a last resort
The rule: physical exam → FBC (not ferritin/hormones/TFTs) → LNG-IUS 1st-line; else tranexamic acid/NSAIDs (no contraception) or COCP/progestogens (contraception); surgery if medical fails + family complete. Treat the cause (iron for anaemia; fibroids/adenomyosis/coagulopathy specifically).
Exam Pearls
Definition
Bleeding that impairs quality of life — impact-based, not a millilitre threshold. “DUB” is obsolete.
PALM-COEIN
Structural (Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy) vs non-structural (Coagulopathy, Ovulatory, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not-classified).
Investigations
FBC for everyone (anaemia) — but NOT routine ferritin, hormones, or TFTs. HMB since menarche + bleeding history → test for coagulopathy (von Willebrand).
Exam
Physical exam before investigations or LNG-IUS fitting.
Management
1st-line = LNG-IUS; else tranexamic acid/NSAIDs (no contraception; NSAIDs if pain too) or COCP/cyclical progestogens (contraception wanted); surgery (ablation/hysterectomy) if medical fails.
Red flag
Intermenstrual/postcoital/postmenopausal bleeding → exclude malignancy (hysteroscopy + biopsy).
What & Why

Dysmenorrhoea = painful menstruation — the commonest cause of school/work absence in adolescent girls. The whole approach hinges on separating primary (no pathology — treat symptomatically) from secondary (a pelvic disease is causing it — find + treat the cause).

Mechanism (primary): the endometrium releases prostaglandins (esp. PGF2α) → myometrial contractions + uterine ischaemia → cramping pain. This is why NSAIDs (prostaglandin-synthesis inhibitors) are first-line + so effective.
The Decisive Fork — Primary vs Secondary
PrimarySecondary
CauseNo pathology (prostaglandin-driven)Underlying pelvic pathology
OnsetYoung — 6–12 months after menarcheOlder — 20s–30s+, often after years of pain-free periods
TimingWith or just before the period, lasts 1–3 daysOften begins days before; persists through + after; may occur at other times
FeaturesNone (± nausea, headache, backache)Deep dyspareunia, menorrhagia, intermenstrual/postcoital bleeding, subfertility
ExaminationNormalMay be abnormal (mass, tenderness, fixed uterus)
Secondary causes: endometriosis (classic — cyclical pain, dyspareunia, subfertility), adenomyosis (boggy tender uterus, HMB), fibroids, PID (esp. new-onset in under-25s — chlamydia), ovarian cysts, copper IUD (iatrogenic), cervical stenosis/outflow anomalies.
Assessment & Investigations
History: age of onset (vs menarche), timing/pattern, associated symptoms (dyspareunia, HMB, intermenstrual/postcoital bleeding, subfertility, discharge/fever → PID), impact, contraception (copper coil). Examination: primary → defer/normal; secondary suspected → abdominal + pelvic (bimanual/speculum) exam for masses, tenderness, a fixed/retroverted uterus, adnexal masses.
Investigations (if secondary suspected): pregnancy test (exclude ectopic); STI screen / high vaginal + endocervical swabs (PID/chlamydia, esp. under-25s); transvaginal ultrasound (fibroids, adenomyosis, cysts, endometrioma); laparoscopy = gold standard for endometriosis (but empirical medical treatment first is supported). Primary needs none if the history is typical.
Management
🩹 Primary — stepwise ladder
  • 1st-line: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) from onset of pain — inhibit prostaglandins; ± paracetamol
  • 2nd-line: hormonal — COCP (cyclical or extended/tricycling; check UKMEC); LNG-IUS/progestogen alternatives
  • Combination (NSAID + hormonal) if single agents insufficient
  • Non-drug: local heat, TENS, gentle exercise
🎯 Secondary — treat the cause
  • Endometriosis → analgesia → hormonal suppression (COCP/progestogen) → GnRH analogues → laparoscopic surgery
  • PID → antibiotics; fibroids/adenomyosis → cause-specific; copper coil → consider removal/alternative
  • Refer to gynaecology if specialist workup needed or symptoms severe
Mefenamic acid is now less favoured as the NSAID of choice (no better efficacy, narrow therapeutic window, higher seizure risk in overdose) — ibuprofen/naproxen preferred. Key rule: failure to respond to NSAIDs + hormonal contraception → suspect a secondary cause (esp. endometriosis) → investigate/refer.
Exam Pearls
Primary
No pathology, prostaglandin-driven, starts 6–12 months after menarche, pain with the period, normal exam.
Secondary
Underlying pathology, older onset, pain precedes/outlasts the period, associated symptoms (dyspareunia, HMB), abnormal exam.
Secondary causes
Endometriosis (classic), adenomyosis, fibroids, PID (under-25s), ovarian cysts, copper IUD.
Treatment
Primary: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) → COCP; combine if needed. Non-drug: heat + TENS.
Mefenamic acid
No longer the preferred NSAID (seizure risk in overdose, narrow window).
Rules
Failure to respond to NSAIDs + hormonal → suspect endometriosis → investigate. Secondary → treat the cause. New pelvic pain in under-25s → think PID/chlamydia.
What & Why

Amenorrhoea = absence of menstruation — a symptom, not a diagnosis. Work backwards through the axis: hypothalamus (GnRH) → pituitary (FSH/LH) → ovaries (oestrogen) → endometrium → patent outflow tract. A break at any level causes amenorrhoea, and the FSH/LH pattern tells you where. Always exclude pregnancy first.

The Decisive Fork — Primary vs Secondary
PrimarySecondary
DefinitionNEVER established menstruationMenstruation stopped after being established
ThresholdNo period by 15 (with normal secondary sexual characteristics) OR by 13 (with none)3–6 months if previously regular; 6–12 months if previous oligomenorrhoea
👶 Primary causes

  • Androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY, female phenotype)
  • Outflow malformations — imperforate hymen, transverse septum, Müllerian agenesis (MRKH)
  • Functional hypothalamic (anorexia); congenital adrenal hyperplasia; constitutional delay
🌸 Secondary causes
  • Pregnancy/lactation/menopause (exclude first)
  • Hypothalamic — stress, excessive exercise, low weight/anorexia (↓GnRH → hypogonadotropic)
  • PCOS (commonest pathological cause)
  • Hyperprolactinaemia; POI; thyroid disease
  • Sheehan's (pituitary necrosis after PPH); Asherman's (intrauterine adhesions after D&C)
Investigations
Always first: exclude pregnancy (β-hCG). Blood panel: FBC, U&E, TFTs, coeliac screen. Then the key hormones localise the lesion:

Management & Exam Pearls
📷 Image placeholder — PCOS Rotterdam criteria — 2 of 3: oligo/anovulation, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on transvaginal ultrasound
Treat the underlying cause: gonadal dysgenesis/POI → HRT (secondary sexual characteristics + bone); hypothalamic → weight restoration, reduce exercise, manage stress/eating disorder + bone protection; PCOS → weight management, cycle regulation (COCP/progestogen for endometrial protection), treat hyperandrogenism/subfertility; hyperprolactinaemia → dopamine agonist (cabergoline/bromocriptine); outflow obstruction (imperforate hymen) → surgery; Asherman's → hysteroscopic adhesiolysis.
First step
Always exclude pregnancy (β-hCG). Amenorrhoea is a symptom.
Thresholds
Primary: no period by 15 (with) or 13 (without secondary sexual characteristics). Secondary: 3–6 months (regular) or 6–12 months (oligomenorrhoea).
FSH/LH
LOW = hypothalamic/pituitary; HIGH = ovarian (POI, Turner's) → check karyotype if high.
Commonest causes
Primary = gonadal dysgenesis (Turner's, 45,XO); pathological secondary = PCOS.
Hypothalamic
Low weight / over-exercise / stress → ↓GnRH → low FSH/LH (“the athlete”).
Eponyms
Sheehan's = pituitary necrosis after PPH; Asherman's = intrauterine adhesions after D&C → hysteroscopic adhesiolysis. Raised prolactin → repeat then pituitary MRI. Turner's/POI → HRT.
What & Why

Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) = psychological, physical + behavioural symptoms in the LUTEAL phase (the ~2 weeks before the period) that resolve once menstruation starts. Common (~40%); ~5–8% severe; the severest form is premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) — a recognised psychiatric diagnosis.

Core concept: symptoms are triggered by normal cyclical ovarian hormone CHANGES (not abnormal levels) — susceptible women over-respond to the fluctuations. This is why suppressing ovulation (COCP, GnRH) and modulating serotonin (SSRIs) both work.
The Decisive Fork — Is the Timing Cyclical & Luteal?
PMS / PMDDA primary mood disorder
TimingSymptoms only in the luteal phase, resolve with menstruation, a symptom-free week after the periodPresent throughout the cycle, no symptom-free interval
DiagnosisProspective symptom diary over 2 cycles confirms the patternDiagnosed on its own criteria
The key teaching point: PMS is defined by the cyclical pattern, confirmed PROSPECTIVELY — not by symptoms alone (retrospective recall over-diagnoses it). If symptoms don't clear after the period, it's NOT PMS.
PMS vs PMDD; Symptoms & Diagnosis (RCOG GTG48)
🔤 PMS vs PMDD + symptoms
  • PMS = the broad syndrome (physical + psychological + behavioural, luteal)
  • PMDD = the severe, predominantly affective form — a formal psychiatric diagnosis (DSM-5/ICD-11)
  • Psychological: mood swings, irritability, depression, anxiety, tension
  • Physical: breast tenderness, bloating, headache, fatigue, cravings
  • Behavioural: poor concentration, sleep disturbance, withdrawal
🔬 Diagnosis
  • Prospective symptom diary over 2 cycles — the DRSP (Daily Record of Severity of Problems) is RCOG-recommended
  • Must show symptoms confined to the luteal phase + a symptom-free interval
  • Exclude other diagnoses (depression/bipolar, thyroid, perimenopause)
  • If unclear → a 3-month GnRH-analogue trial (switches off ovarian hormones; resolution confirms it's ovulation-driven)
Management — the Stepped Ladder (RCOG GTG48)
StepTreatment
1st-lineLifestyle (exercise, sleep, diet, reduce alcohol/caffeine) + CBT; continuous drospirenone COCP (e.g. Yasmin) to suppress ovulation; SSRIs (citalopram/escitalopram) — continuous OR luteal-phase only (rapid onset in PMS) — for moderate–severe/PMDD
2nd-lineHigher-dose SSRIs (continuous/luteal), or transdermal oestradiol + progestogen (for endometrial protection)
3rd-line (specialist)GnRH analogues — potent ovulation suppression → hypo-oestrogenic → require “add-back” HRT (protect bone/cardiovascular); severe/resistant only
4th-line (last resort)Hysterectomy + bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (± HRT) — removes ovarian cycling; most severe/resistant, family complete
Other options: spironolactone (bloating/breast tenderness), some evidence for vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), CBT throughout. The ladder's logic: you're either suppressing ovulation (COCP → GnRH → surgery, escalating potency) or modulating serotonin (SSRIs) — the two mechanistic levers.
Exam Pearls
Definition
Cyclical luteal-phase symptoms that RESOLVE with menstruation — a symptom-free week after the period is essential.
Diagnosis
Prospective symptom diary (DRSP) over 2 cycles. If symptoms don't clear after the period → not PMS.
PMDD
The severe, predominantly mood-based form — a formal psychiatric diagnosis.
1st-line
Lifestyle/CBT + continuous drospirenone COCP + SSRIs (continuous or luteal-phase — a distinctive point, rapid onset).
Escalation
Diagnostic uncertainty → 3-month GnRH-analogue trial; GnRH analogues (3rd-line) need add-back HRT (protect bone).
Levers / trap
Two levers: suppress ovulation (COCP→GnRH→surgery) or modulate serotonin (SSRI). Don't confuse with depression/bipolar (present throughout the cycle).
OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Infections in:
What & Why

HIV in pregnancy is a prevention-of-vertical-transmission topic — stop the virus passing from mother to baby. With the full care bundle, UK vertical transmission is <0.5% (down from ~25% untreated).

Vertical transmission happens at three points: in utero (placenta), intrapartum (the BIGGEST risk — exposure to maternal blood/secretions at delivery), and postnatally (breastfeeding). Each intervention targets one route.
Above all, know the one number that drives decisions: the maternal VIRAL LOAD.
The Decisive Fork — Maternal Viral Load (BHIVA, Guideline-Verified)
📷 Image placeholder — HIV mode-of-delivery flow — maternal viral load near 36 weeks (<50 → vaginal + neonatal monotherapy; ≥400 → planned caesarean + combination PEP)
Viral load (≈36 weeks)Mode of deliveryNeonatal PEP
<50 copies/mL (suppressed)Vaginal delivery supportedLow-risk: usually zidovudine monotherapy (short course)
50–399 copies/mLConsider caesareanHigher-risk: combination PEP
≥400 copies/mLPlanned caesarean recommendedHigher-risk: combination PEP
The organising principle: an undetectable viral load (<50) is the target — it makes vaginal birth safe + minimises neonatal treatment. A detectable/high viral load shifts everything toward caesarean + intensified infant prophylaxis.
Antenatal Screening
HIV testing is offered to ALL pregnant women at booking (opt-out) — alongside hepatitis B + syphilis. This universal screening is the foundation of the low UK transmission rate. Late presenters/untested women in labour → urgent point-of-care testing.
Management — the Care Bundle
💊 Maternal antiretroviral therapy (ART)
  • ALL pregnant women with HIV take combination ART, for life — regardless of CD4 or viral load
  • Already on effective ART at conception → continue it
  • Newly diagnosed → start ASAP (suppress before delivery)
  • Typical: tenofovir + emtricitabine (or abacavir + lamivudine) + a third agent, often dolutegravir
🏥 Mode of delivery
  • Determined by viral load at ~36 weeks (table above)
  • <50 → vaginal supported; ≥400 → planned caesarean
  • IV zidovudine infusion intrapartum if caesarean for viral-load reasons / higher-risk labour
  • Avoid fetal scalp electrodes, fetal blood sampling, instrumental delivery if not suppressed
👶 Neonatal PEP
  • Every exposed infant gets antiretroviral PEP, within 4 hours of birth
  • Low-risk (mother <50) → zidovudine monotherapy (~2–4 weeks)
  • Higher-risk (detectable/unknown viral load) → combination PEP
🍼 Infant feeding + diagnosis
  • UK default = FORMULA feeding (eliminates the breastfeeding route)
  • BHIVA now supports breastfeeding if strict criteria met: fully suppressed (<50), good adherence, MDT engagement, monthly viral-load monitoring (mother + baby)
  • Diagnose infant with HIV PCR (viral, not antibody — maternal antibodies persist ~18 months)
Exam Pearls
Goal
Prevent vertical transmission; full bundle → UK rate <0.5%.
Screening
HIV test offered to ALL pregnant women (opt-out) at booking — with hep B + syphilis.
The magic number
Viral load <50 (undetectable) allows vaginal birth + simplest infant PEP; ≥400 → planned caesarean; 50–399 → consider caesarean.
ART
All pregnant women with HIV take ART for life — commonly tenofovir/emtricitabine + dolutegravir.
Neonatal PEP
Every exposed baby within 4 hours — zidovudine monotherapy if mother suppressed, combination if higher-risk.
Feeding / diagnosis
UK default = formula; breastfeeding only if fully suppressed + strict MDT monitoring. Diagnose the infant with HIV PCR, not antibody.
Routes
Placenta, delivery (biggest), breastfeeding — each intervention maps to one.
What & Why

Chickenpox in pregnancy = primary infection with varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in a susceptible woman. It threatens two patients: the mother (varicella is far more dangerous in adults/pregnancy — pneumonia, hepatitis, encephalitis) and the fetus/neonate (fetal varicella syndrome, or neonatal varicella).

~90% of UK adults are already immune → most exposures are harmless; danger is confined to the non-immune (seronegative) minority. VZV is highly contagious (droplets/contact); shingles can transmit varicella to a non-immune person. The varicella vaccine is live → contraindicated in pregnancy.
The Decisive Fork — Immune or Not? Rash or Not?
1️⃣ Is she immune?
  • Prior chickenpox / 2 doses of vaccine → reassure, no action
  • No/uncertain history → check VZV IgG serology urgently → if seronegative, proceed
2️⃣ Exposure vs established rash?
  • Susceptible + exposure, NO rash yet → post-exposure prophylaxis (antiviral) — attenuate/prevent maternal disease
  • Rash already developed → oral (or IV) aciclovir; NOT VZIG
The single most-tested trap: VZIG is USELESS once the rash is out. It's a prophylactic, not a treatment → established chickenpox is treated with aciclovir, never VZIG.
Maternal & Fetal/Neonatal Risks
Maternal (more severe in adults/pregnancy): varicella pneumonia (major cause of maternal mortality — risk rises with gestation, smoking, immunosuppression), hepatitis, encephalitis, rare death.
Timing of maternal infectionRisk to baby
<28 weeks (esp. <20 wks)Fetal Varicella Syndrome (FVS) — small overall risk (~1%)
28 weeks – termFetus may develop shingles in infancy; usually well at birth
Around delivery (−7 to +7 days)Neonatal varicella — can be severe/fatal (exposed with no maternal antibody yet)
Fetal Varicella Syndrome: skin scarring in a dermatomal distribution, limb hypoplasia, eye defects (chorioretinitis, cataracts, microphthalmia), neurological abnormalities (microcephaly, learning disability).
Management (RCOG GTG13 / UKHSA — Guideline-Verified)
🛡️ Susceptible + exposure (no rash) — PEP
  • Confirm susceptibility with urgent VZV IgG
  • Antivirals are now preferred PEP — oral aciclovir 800 mg QDS from days 7–14 after exposure (valaciclovir an alternative)
  • Reflects the UKHSA/RCOG shift (no significant difference vs VZIG; avoids VZIG cost/scarcity) — older teaching said “VZIG first”
  • VZIG only if unable to take oral antivirals (malabsorption/renal toxicity)
🔴 Develops the rash
  • Contact GP immediately; avoid contact with pregnant women/neonates until lesions crust (~5 days)
  • Oral aciclovir if within 24h of onset AND ≥20 weeks (caution <20 weeks — counsel)
  • IV aciclovir for severe disease (pneumonia, neuro signs, dense rash) → admit
  • Do NOT give VZIG — no benefit once rash present
Fetal monitoring: refer to fetal medicine; detailed ultrasound ~5 weeks after infection for FVS features (amniocentesis only after skin lesions fully heal). Delivery/neonatal: avoid delivery in the viraemic period (delaying ~7 days after rash lets maternal antibody cross); give neonatal VZIG (± aciclovir) if maternal rash appears 7 days before to 7 days after delivery, or for a susceptible exposed neonate. Breastfeeding encouraged if the mother is well.
Exam Pearls
Check immunity first
VZV IgG. Prior chickenpox / 2 vaccine doses → reassure.
The #1 trap
VZIG has NO benefit once the rash appears — established chickenpox is treated with aciclovir.
PEP shift
PEP is now antiviral-first (aciclovir days 7–14 post-exposure), not VZIG — updated UKHSA/RCOG stance.
Rash treatment
Oral aciclovir if within 24h of onset + ≥20 weeks; IV aciclovir for severe disease. Vaccine is live → contraindicated in pregnancy.
Maternal risk
Pneumonia (main killer), hepatitis, encephalitis.
Fetal
Fetal Varicella Syndrome (<28 wks, ~1%): dermatomal scarring, limb hypoplasia, eye + neuro defects.
Perinatal
Infection −7 to +7 days of delivery → severe neonatal varicella → neonatal VZIG. Isolate until lesions crust (~5 days); shingles can give a non-immune person chickenpox.
What & Why

Rubella in pregnancy matters not for the mother (illness is trivial/asymptomatic) but for the catastrophic damage to the developing fetus — the archetypal teratogenic infection + the reason childhood MMR exists. Now at WHO “elimination” levels in the UK (cases usually imported).

The defining fact: there is NO treatment for rubella in pregnancy + no way to protect the current fetus once the mother is infected → everything rests on prevention through pre-pregnancy MMR. Rubella = a single-stranded RNA togavirus, droplet spread, incubation ~14–21 days.

Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) — the Classic Triad
