🎯 The triad
  • Sensorineural deafness (commonest single feature)
  • Congenital cataracts (± “salt-and-pepper” retinopathy, microphthalmia, glaucoma)
  • Congenital heart disease — classically patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) + pulmonary artery stenosis
➕ Other features
  • Microcephaly + learning disability
  • “Blueberry muffin” rash (dermal haematopoiesis — shared with CMV)
  • Hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, growth restriction
The three congenital-infection triads (high-yield side by side): Rubella → cataracts + PDA + deafness; CMV → periventricular calcification + sensorineural deafness + microcephaly; Toxoplasmosis → hydrocephalus + intracranial calcification + chorioretinitis.
Presentation, Screening & Management
Maternal presentation is often subclinical; when symptomatic — a fine maculopapular rash (face → trunk), postauricular/suboccipital lymphadenopathy (characteristic), low-grade fever, malaise, coryza, arthralgia. Mild + self-limiting — the fetus is the patient.
Antenatal rubella susceptibility screening STOPPED in the UK (England) on 1 April 2016 — the test doesn't protect the current pregnancy, may falsely reassure, and disease is now elimination-level rare (HIV, hepatitis B + syphilis screening continue). If rubella is clinically suspected → serology (IgM acute, IgG past/immune), paired sera/avidity to confirm timing; notify public health.
Management + prevention: NO antiviral treatment — supportive for the mother + counselling on fetal risk (first-trimester confirmed infection → fetal medicine, discuss high CRS risk incl. termination). MMR is a live vaccine → contraindicated in pregnancy; offer non-immune women MMR postnatally (avoid conception for 1 month; can give while breastfeeding). Population strategy = childhood MMR (2 doses); check/vaccinate uncertain-immunity women before conceiving.

What & Why

Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) is a gut + vaginal commensal carried by ~a quarter of pregnant women — harmless to the mother, but the leading cause of severe early-onset neonatal infection (sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis) in the UK.

One intervention at one moment: antibiotics DURING labour to stop the baby being colonised as it passes through the birth canal. Timing is everything — GBS prophylaxis is worthless antenatally + only works intrapartum. GBS lives in the maternal vagina/rectum → baby exposed during vaginal delivery → invasive disease in the first days of life.

The UK Approach — Risk-Factor-Based, NOT Universal Screening
The UK does NOT routinely screen all pregnant women for GBS — IAP is offered on risk factors instead. Rationale: most carriers' babies are born safely, a late swab can't reliably predict disease, and screening everyone would give huge numbers of women unnecessary antibiotics (anaphylaxis + resistance risk).
This contrasts with the USA, which uses universal rectovaginal swab screening at 35–37 weeks — a classic exam-comparison trap. The GBS3 trial (UK cluster-randomised) is evaluating whether to switch to universal screening — “watch this space”.
Who Gets Intrapartum Antibiotics (IAP)? (RCOG GTG36)
💉 Offer IAP if ANY of:
  • Previous baby with invasive GBS disease (offer IAP — no swab needed)
  • GBS detected in the current pregnancy — vaginal/rectal swab OR GBS bacteriuria (any GBS in urine)
  • Preterm labour (<37 weeks)
  • Intrapartum fever ≥38°C (or suspected chorioamnionitis → broad-spectrum antibiotics covering GBS)
  • Prolonged rupture of membranes (a recognised additional risk factor)
Two specifics: GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy → treat at diagnosis (e.g. amoxicillin) AND offer intrapartum IAP. Known GBS colonisation in a previous pregnancy → offer either IAP this labour, OR testing (enriched culture medium, ECM) in late pregnancy with IAP if positive.
Management & Neonatal Care
💊 Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis
  • 1st line: IV benzylpenicillin, ASAP once labour starts, repeated 4-hourly until delivery (adequate dosing before birth matters)
  • Penicillin allergy (non-severe): a cephalosporin (e.g. cefuroxime)
  • Severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis): vancomycin
  • Clindamycin is no longer recommended (rising GBS resistance)
No IAP for a planned caesarean with intact membranes before labour (no passage through the birth canal). Neonatal: babies with adequate IAP + well → routine observation; risk factors but inadequate/no IAP, or signs of infection → observation ± investigation + antibiotics per neonatal early-onset sepsis pathways (NICE). Send an MSU antenatally — GBS bacteriuria here triggers treatment + IAP.

What & Why

Mastitis = inflammation of the breast tissue — most commonly LACTATIONAL — caused either by MILK STASIS (duct obstruction → milk accumulation) OR by INFECTION (Staph aureus commonest). Presents as a painful, red, warm area of breast ± fever.

The core concept — it starts as MILK STASIS, not necessarily infection. When milk isn't removed (poor latch, blocked duct, missed feeds, engorgement) it backs up → the duct/tissue inflames → a painful, red, hot segment. Initially this is sterile/inflammatory → so first-line = EFFECTIVE MILK REMOVAL (continue breastfeeding!), NOT antibiotics. If stasis persists, bacteria (Staph aureus) superinfect it → infective mastitis → antibiotics; if untreated → a breast ABSCESS.
Management logic: (1) always CONTINUE breastfeeding + optimise milk removal (safe + therapeutic); (2) antibiotics only when specific criteria suggest infection; (3) recognise + drain an abscess. Common (~1 in 4); usually first weeks postpartum; unilateral + segmental (wedge-shaped). Reflex: a painful, red, wedge-shaped area of breast in a breastfeeding woman = mastitis → keep feeding + effective milk removal → antibiotics only if unwell/fissured/not improving/culture-positive.

  • Ultrasound if an abscess (fluctuant mass) is suspected
The malignancy caveat: “mastitis” that does NOT resolve with treatment → consider INFLAMMATORY BREAST CANCER (esp. non-lactational or persistent) → refer for assessment.
Management (NICE CKS — Guideline-Verified)
The principle: CONTINUE breastfeeding + EFFECTIVE MILK REMOVAL for ALL; conservative measures first; ANTIBIOTICS (flucloxacillin) only if specific criteria met; abscess → drainage.
🍼 Conservative — for ALL
  • CONTINUE BREASTFEEDING (safe + therapeutic) + effective milk removal (feed frequently, good latch/positioning, express if needed)
  • Breast MASSAGE, HEAT PACKS/warm showers, ANALGESIA (paracetamol/ibuprofen)
  • Removing milk IS the treatment
💊 Antibiotics — flucloxacillin, ONLY if:
  • Systemically UNWELL
  • Infected nipple FISSURE
  • Symptoms DON'T improve after 12–24h of effective milk removal
  • Culture indicates infection

Breast abscess (untreated mastitis → fluctuant, very tender pus collection): INCISION & DRAINAGE or ultrasound-guided needle ASPIRATION (increasingly first-line) + antibiotics; keep expressing/feeding.
The rule: ALL — continue breastfeeding + effective milk removal + heat/massage/analgesia → FLUCLOXACILLIN only if (unwell / infected nipple fissure / no improvement in 12–24h / positive culture) → abscess → drainage + antibiotics.

What & Why

Breast engorgement = painful, over-full, swollen breasts in the early postnatal period — from milk accumulation + interstitial oedema + increased blood flow when the milk “comes in”. Typically BILATERAL, in the first few DAYS after birth, and worst just before a feed.

The core concept — supply outstrips removal in the early days. Around days 2–5 postpartum the milk “comes in” (lactogenesis II) → the breasts fill rapidly; if milk isn't removed (infrequent feeds, poor latch), they become overfull, swollen, tense + painful. The key trap: engorgement is benign + self-limiting but mimics early MASTITIS — it can cause redness + a transient low-grade fever — but unlike mastitis it's BILATERAL, diffuse, and settles within ~24h with effective milk removal.
Managed entirely by effective, frequent milk removal (continue breastfeeding); untreated engorgement can PROGRESS to blocked ducts + mastitis. Reflex: bilateral, painful, swollen, full breasts in the first few days postpartum, worst before feeds = engorgement → frequent effective feeding/expression.

  • Pain/discomfort WORST just before a feed

  • May have fever (subsides in ~24h); breast may be red

  • Complications: blocked ducts → MASTITIS, difficulty breastfeeding, and reduced milk supply (unrelieved fullness down-regulates production)
The rule: bilateral, painful, swollen, full breasts in the first few days postpartum, worst before feeds, with poor milk flow + difficult infant attachment ± a transient fever = engorgement.
Management
The principle: effective, frequent MILK REMOVAL (continue breastfeeding) is the treatment; support latch/attachment; symptomatic relief; it's self-limiting.
🍼 Milk removal + latch
  • CONTINUE breastfeeding — feed frequently + on demand (don't restrict/delay); ensure effective milk removal
  • Express a little if too full/tense for the baby to attach
  • Support good positioning/latch; REVERSE PRESSURE SOFTENING (gently press the areola to soften it) → helps the baby latch
🧊 Symptomatic relief
  • Analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen — safe in breastfeeding)
  • WARM compress/shower BEFORE a feed (encourages let-down); COLD compress AFTER (reduces swelling)
  • ± gentle breast massage; reassure — benign + self-limiting
The rule: continue frequent breastfeeding + effective milk removal + support latch (express to soften the areola) + analgesia + warm-before/cold-after compresses; self-limiting → reassure; prevents progression to mastitis.

What & Why

Galactocele = a benign, milk-filled RETENTION CYST of the breast — from occlusion of a lactiferous duct → milk builds up behind the blockage → a cystic lesion. Typically occurs in women who have recently STOPPED (or reduced) breastfeeding, and is characteristically PAINLESS with NO signs of infection.

The core concept — “trapped milk in a cyst”: a lactiferous duct blocks, milk accumulates behind it + gets walled off into a smooth cystic lesion. The single key point is that it is BENIGN + PAINLESS + NON-infected — exactly what distinguishes it from the other lactational lumps (mastitis: painful, red, hot, febrile; abscess: painful, fluctuant, unwell). It classically appears as breastfeeding winds down (milk removal falls but some milk is still produced → a duct occludes → milk pools).
Task: recognise the typical benign presentation → confirm with ultrasound → reassure — while keeping the usual caution that any breast lump needs its diagnosis confirmed. Reflex: a painless, smooth breast lump in a woman who has recently stopped breastfeeding, with no signs of infection = galactocele.

Overview — The Menstrual Cycle
The menstrual cycle is the ~28-day hormonal cycle that prepares the body for pregnancy each month — coordinating ovarian events (follicle → ovulation → corpus luteum) with uterine events (endometrial proliferation → secretion → shedding).
The organising principle: it's the HPG axis running cyclically — driven by the interplay of FSH/LH (pituitary) and oestrogen/progesterone (ovary), governed by negative feedback except for the one mid-cycle positive-feedback burst that triggers ovulation. Two parallel cycles run together: the ovarian cycle and the uterine (endometrial) cycle.
Why it matters: underpins contraception, ovulation/fertility, menstrual disorders, pregnancy, and the hormonal blood tests — cross-ref sex hormones & reproductive axes (the HPG axis), contraception, PCOS, pregnancy physiology, infertility.
The Two Parallel Cycles — ovary + uterus, linked by hormones

The link: the ovarian hormones drive the uterine changes — oestrogen (follicular) → proliferation; progesterone (luteal) → secretory preparation; their withdrawal → menstruation.
The Phases in Sequence — follow the ~28-day cycle
Follicular phase (days ~1–14) — oestrogen-dominant, variable length
  • FSH rises → stimulates follicle development (several recruited, one becomes dominant)
  • The growing follicle (granulosa cells) produces rising oestrogen
  • Oestrogen → endometrial proliferation (thickening — the proliferative phase) + thins cervical mucus (fertile)
  • Feedback: through most of this phase, oestrogen gives negative feedback (keeps FSH/LH in check); FSH falls slightly (selecting the dominant follicle)
Ovulation (~day 14) — the LH surge, the positive-feedback exception
  • As the dominant follicle matures, oestrogen peaks → at a critical high level, feedback switches to positive → triggers a massive LH surge (+ smaller FSH surge)
  • The LH surge → ovulation (the follicle ruptures, releasing the egg ~24–36h after the surge begins)
The positive-feedback point (high-yield): this is the only positive-feedback loop in the cycle (and one of the few in endocrinology) — high oestrogen stimulates rather than suppresses LH → the ovulatory trigger.
Luteal phase (days ~14–28) — progesterone-dominant, fixed ~14 days
  • After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum → secretes progesterone (+ some oestrogen)
  • Progesterone → secretory endometrium (glands secrete, prepares for implantation) + thickens cervical mucus + raises basal body temperature (the ovulation marker)
  • Feedback: progesterone + oestrogen suppress FSH/LH (negative feedback → prevents new follicles during the luteal phase)
The fixed length: the luteal phase is reliably ~14 days (the corpus luteum has a fixed lifespan) → so cycle-length variation comes from the follicular phase, not the luteal (useful for dating ovulation).
Menstruation (days ~1–5) — hormone withdrawal
  • If no pregnancy: the corpus luteum regresses (~day 24–28) → progesterone + oestrogen fall → the endometrium can't be maintained → sheds (menstruation)
  • The falling hormones release the feedback → FSH rises again → the next cycle begins
The Hormone Pattern — the high-yield summary

The two key events to anchor: the mid-cycle oestrogen peak → LH surge → ovulation, and the luteal progesterone rise → secretory endometrium (then its fall → menstruation).
If Pregnancy Occurs — the cycle's purpose
  • If the egg is fertilised + implants → the embryo secretes hCG → rescues the corpus luteum → progesterone is maintained → the endometrium is preserved (no menstruation) → pregnancy continues
hCG is the basis of pregnancy tests + maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over progesterone production (~weeks 8–12) — cross-ref pregnancy/placental physiology.

Overview — Pregnancy Physiology
Pregnancy demands enormous maternal physiological adaptations — to support the growing fetus, prepare for birth, and protect the mother — affecting nearly every organ system.
The organising principle: the maternal body adapts to (1) supply the fetus (↑cardiac output, ↑blood volume, ↑ventilation) and (2) prepare for delivery + lactation — driven by pregnancy hormones (hCG, progesterone, oestrogen, hPL). Many "abnormal-looking" findings are normal adaptations, and knowing them explains the pregnancy-specific diseases.
Why it matters: explains the normal changes (and why some bloods/obs shift), gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, the anaemia of pregnancy, VTE risk, and physiological breathlessness — cross-ref the menstrual cycle (hCG/corpus luteum), placental physiology, sex hormones, gestational diabetes/pre-eclampsia, drugs in pregnancy.

Haematological Adaptations — the "physiological anaemia" (high-yield)
  • ↑Plasma volume (~50%) > ↑red cell mass (~25%) → the blood is diluted → physiological (dilutional) anaemia of pregnancy (a normal drop in Hb, not iron deficiency)
  • Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state: ↑clotting factors + ↓fibrinolysis + venous stasis → ↑VTE risk (Virchow's triad — cross-ref) → why VTE is a leading cause of maternal death and why prophylaxis matters
  • ↑Iron + folate requirements (fetal demand) → iron + folate supplementation (folate also prevents neural tube defects — cross-ref drugs in pregnancy)
Respiratory Adaptations — physiological breathlessness
  • ↑Tidal volume → ↑minute ventilation (progesterone-driven) → blows off CO₂ → mild respiratory alkalosis (compensated by renal HCO₃⁻ excretion)
  • The breathlessness point: many pregnant women feel breathless (the ↑ventilation + the uterus splinting the diaphragm) — usually physiological, but must be distinguished from PE (given the ↑VTE risk)
  • O₂ consumption rises (fetal + maternal demand)
Renal Adaptations
  • ↑Renal blood flow + ↑GFR (~50%) → ↓serum creatinine + urea (so a "normal" creatinine may actually be relatively high in pregnancy)
  • Physiological hydronephrosis (progesterone → ureteric smooth muscle relaxation + uterine compression) → urinary stasis → ↑UTI/pyelonephritis risk
  • Mild glycosuria (lowered renal threshold — cross-ref tubular reabsorption) — usually benign
Metabolic & Endocrine Adaptations — the gestational diabetes link (high-yield)
  • ↑Insulin resistance (driven by hPL, progesterone, cortisol) → diverts glucose across the placenta to the fetus
  • The clinical link: if the maternal pancreas can't compensate for this insulin resistance → gestational diabetes (cross-ref) → the physiological reason GDM emerges in the later trimesters (when hPL/placental hormones peak)
  • Thyroid: ↑thyroid binding globulin (oestrogen) + hCG stimulates the thyroid → ↑demand (why thyroxine doses ↑ in pregnancy)
  • Weight gain, ↑appetite, fat storage (early) → mobilisation (late, for the fetus)
Other Adaptations
  • GI: progesterone relaxes smooth muscle → ↓gut motility (constipation), ↓LOS tone (reflux/heartburn), gallbladder stasis (gallstones); nausea/vomiting (hCG-related)
  • Uterus: massive growth (smooth muscle hypertrophy)
  • Breast: oestrogen/progesterone → ductal + glandular development (preparing for lactation — cross-ref)
  • Skin: pigmentation (melasma, linea nigra)

Overview — Placental & Fetal Physiology
The placenta is the fetus's lifeline — it does the jobs the fetal lungs, gut, kidneys, and liver can't yet do (gas exchange, nutrition, waste removal) and acts as the main endocrine organ of pregnancy; the fetal circulation is uniquely adapted to a placenta-dependent, lung-bypassing existence.
The organising principle: before birth, the placenta does everything and the lungs do nothing → so the fetal circulation has shunts that bypass the lungs and liver; at birth, the first breath flips this → the shunts close and the adult circulation takes over. Understanding the shunts explains congenital heart disease and the transition at birth.
Why it matters: underpins the fetal circulation + its changes at birth, congenital heart defects (PDA, ASD), the placental hormones, fetal-maternal transfer (drugs, antibodies, rhesus disease), and fetal haemoglobin — cross-ref pregnancy physiology, O₂ dissociation curve (HbF), immunity (passive transfer), drugs in pregnancy, congenital heart disease.

Fetal Haemoglobin — the oxygen adaptation
  • Fetal haemoglobin (HbF, 2α2γ) has a higher O₂ affinity than adult HbA (left-shifted dissociation curve — cross-ref O₂ dissociation note) → lets the fetus extract O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta (fetal Hb grabs O₂ that maternal Hb releases)
  • HbF is gradually replaced by adult HbA after birth (which is why β-chain disorders like sickle cell/β-thalassaemia present after birth, as HbF wanes — cross-ref red cell physiology)
The Fetal Circulation — the lung-bypassing design (core)
Before birth, the lungs are fluid-filled and non-functional → the circulation is designed to bypass the lungs and liver using three shunts, with oxygenated blood coming from the placenta:
Shunt Connects Purpose
Ductus venosusUmbilical vein → IVCBypasses the liver (sends placental blood straight to the heart)
Foramen ovaleRight atrium → left atriumBypasses the lungs (shunts blood across the atria)
Ductus arteriosusPulmonary artery → aortaBypasses the lungs (diverts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta)
The flow logic: oxygenated blood from the placenta (umbilical vein) → ductus venosus (past liver) → IVC → right atrium → most crosses the foramen ovale to the left heart → to the body/brain; blood entering the pulmonary artery mostly crosses the ductus arteriosus to the aorta (since the high-resistance fluid-filled lungs are bypassed).
The key principle: high pulmonary vascular resistance (fluid-filled lungs) + low systemic resistance (the large placental circulation) → drives blood away from the lungs and through the shunts.
The Transition at Birth — the flip (high-yield)
The first breath transforms the circulation in minutes:
  • Lungs inflate → pulmonary vascular resistance falls dramatically → blood now flows into the lungs
  • Cord clamped → loss of the low-resistance placenta → systemic vascular resistance rises
  • These pressure changes close the shunts:
Shunt Closes to become Trigger
Foramen ovaleFossa ovalisLeft atrial pressure now > right → flap closes
Ductus arteriosusLigamentum arteriosum↑O₂ + ↓prostaglandins → constricts (closes over days)
Ductus venosusLigamentum venosumLoss of umbilical flow
The prostaglandin point (high-yield): the ductus arteriosus is kept open by prostaglandins in utero → after birth, ↑O₂ + ↓prostaglandins close it → so prostaglandins (PGE) keep it open (used in duct-dependent congenital heart disease) and NSAIDs/indometacin close it (used in patent ductus arteriosus).

Overview — Lactation
Lactation = the production and release of breast milk — prepared during pregnancy, established after birth, and maintained by suckling.
The organising principle: lactation has two hormonal arms — prolactin makes the milk (production/synthesis) and oxytocin ejects it (the let-down reflex) — both sustained by the suckling stimulus. Pregnancy primes the breast but high hormones prevent milk release until birth removes the block.
Why it matters: explains breastfeeding physiology, why milk only flows after delivery, lactational amenorrhoea, drugs in breast milk, and prolactin-related conditions — cross-ref sex hormones (prolactin/oxytocin, the HP axis), pregnancy physiology, the immunity note (breast-milk IgA).
The Two Hormones — make vs eject (the spine)
Hormone Source Role
ProlactinAnterior pituitaryMilk production/synthesis (the "make" hormone)
OxytocinPosterior pituitaryMilk ejection / let-down (the "eject" hormone — contracts myoepithelial cells)
The clean division: prolactin = production, oxytocin = ejection — get these two straight and lactation makes sense.
Breast Preparation in Pregnancy — priming (and why milk doesn't flow yet)
  • During pregnancy, oestrogen + progesterone (placental) → develop the ducts + alveoli (glandular tissue) → the breast is prepared for milk production
The key paradox (high-yield): prolactin rises through pregnancy, but the high oestrogen + progesterone block prolactin's milk-producing action → so no milk is made during pregnancy despite the priming.
The trigger at birth: delivery of the placenta → oestrogen + progesterone fall sharply → removes the block → prolactin can now act → milk production begins (~day 2–3 postpartum) — explains why milk "comes in" a couple of days after birth.
(Colostrum — the protein/antibody-rich first milk — is produced in the first few days before mature milk.)
Prolactin & Milk Production — the maintenance loop (high-yield)
  • Prolactin drives milk synthesis in the alveolar cells
  • The suckling reflex (the maintenance mechanism): the baby suckling → sensory signal to the hypothalamus → ↑prolactin (and ↑oxytocin) → more milk made (and ejected) → supply matches demand ("supply and demand")
The dopamine control point (ties to the HP axis): prolactin is normally under tonic inhibition by dopamine (cross-ref sex hormones) → suckling reduces dopamine inhibition → prolactin rises; this is also why dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics) ↑prolactin (→ galactorrhoea) and dopamine agonists (bromocriptine/cabergoline) suppress lactation.
Oxytocin & the Let-Down Reflex — milk ejection (high-yield)
  • Oxytocin causes the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli to contract → ejects milk into the ducts (the "let-down" reflex)
  • The let-down reflex: suckling → hypothalamus → posterior pituitary releases oxytocin → milk ejection
The neuroendocrine point (high-yield): let-down can be triggered by the baby's cry or the sight of the baby (a conditioned/neural reflex), and inhibited by stress/pain (sympathetic) → which is why a relaxed environment aids breastfeeding.
Oxytocin also causes uterine contraction → so breastfeeding helps involute the uterus postpartum (and can cause "afterpains").
Lactational Amenorrhoea — the contraceptive effect (high-yield)
  • High prolactin suppresses the HPG axis (↓GnRH → ↓LH/FSH) → suppresses ovulation → lactational amenorrhoea (a natural, though unreliable, contraceptive effect during exclusive breastfeeding)
  • This is why breastfeeding delays the return of menstruation/fertility postpartum
Breast Milk — the immunity link
  • Colostrum (first few days): protein- and antibody-rich (esp. IgA)
  • Mature milk: balanced nutrition + immune protection
The immunity link (high-yield): breast milk provides secretory IgA → mucosal protection for the neonate's gut/respiratory tract = natural passive immunity (cross-ref immunity note's active/passive 2×2).

Two hormones
Prolactin (anterior pituitary) = milk production; oxytocin (posterior pituitary) = milk ejection (let-down).

Suckling reflex
Maintains both prolactin (production) + oxytocin (ejection) → supply matches demand.
Dopamine control
Prolactin under dopamine inhibition → dopamine antagonists ↑prolactin; dopamine agonists (cabergoline) suppress lactation.
Let-down (oxytocin)
Triggered by suckling/baby's cry, inhibited by stress; oxytocin also → uterine involution.
Amenorrhoea & immunity
High prolactin suppresses HPG → ovulation suppressed (natural contraception); breast milk = IgA → neonatal passive immunity (colostrum antibody-rich).
